senses.d: A child's word for mother.
In Oriental countries, a respectful form of address given to a woman; mother.
But; — used in cautionary phrases; as, “Vivace, ma non troppo presto” (i.e., lively, but not too quick).
The common European gull (Larus canus); — called also mar. See New, a gull.
Belonging, or relating, to Macedonia.
A native or inhabitant of Macedonia.

One of a certain religious sect, followers of Macedonius, Bishop of Constantinople, in the fourth century, who held that the Holy Ghost was a creature, like the angels, and a servant of the Father and the Son.
Disordered in intellect; crazy; insane.
q: I have heard my grandsire say full oft, Extremity of griefs would make men mad.

senses.d: Excited beyond self-control or the restraint of reason; inflamed by violent or uncontrollable desire, passion, or appetite; as, to be mad with terror, lust, or hatred; mad against political reform.
q: It is the land of graven images, and they are mad upon their idols.
And being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange cities.

senses.d: Proceeding from, or indicating, madness; expressing distraction; prompted by infatuation, fury, or extreme rashness.
q: Mad wars destroy in one year the works of many years of peace.
The mad promise of Cleon was fulfilled.

senses.d: Extravagant; immoderate.
Furious with rage, terror, or disease; — said of the lower animals; as, a mad bull; esp., having hydrophobia; rabid; as, a mad dog.
Angry; out of patience; vexed; as, to get mad at a person.
Having impaired polarity; — applied to a compass needle.

Mad.etym: [AS. gem�d, gemād, mad; akin to OS. gem�d foolish, OHG. gameit, Icel. mei�a to hurt, Goth. gamáids weak, broken. �.]

senses.d: To make mad or furious; to madden.
q: Had I but seen thy picture in this plight, It would have madded me.

senses.d: To be mad; to go mad; to rave. See Madding.
q: Festus said with great voice, Paul thou maddest.

senses.d: An earthworm.

Mad.etym: [AS. ma�a; akin to D. & G. made, Goth. mapa, and prob. to E. moth.]

senses.d: Artificially produced; pieced together; formed by filling in; as, made ground; a made mast, in distinction from one consisting of a single spar.
The condition of being mad; insanity; lunacy.
Frenzy; ungovernable rage; extreme folly.

Madness.syn: Insanity; distraction; derangement; craziness; lunacy; mania; frenzy; franticness; rage; aberration; alienation; monomania. See Insanity.

senses.d: Designating an orange-red dyestuff obtained from naphthylamine, and called magdala red, naphthalene red, etc.
One skilled in magic; one who practices the black art; an enchanter; a necromancer; a sorcerer or sorceress; a conjurer.
A person clothed with power as a public civil officer; a public civil officer invested with the executive government, or some branch of it.
q: Of magistrates some also are supreme, in whom the sovereign power of the state resides; others are subordinate.

Magistrate.etym: [L. magistratus, fr. magister master: cf. F. magistrat. See Master.]

senses.d: The act of doing what is magnificent; the state or quality of being magnificent.
q: And, for the heaven's wide circuit, let it speak The Maker's high magnificence, who built so spacious.
The noblest monuments of Roman magnificence.

senses.d: To make great, or greater; to increase the dimensions of; to amplify; to enlarge, either in fact or in appearance; as, the microscope magnifies the object by a thousand diameters.
q: The least error in a small quantity . . . will in a great one . . . be proportionately magnified.

senses.d: To increase the importance of; to augment the esteem or respect in which one is held.
q: On that day the Lord magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel.

senses.d: To praise highly; to laud; to extol.
q: O, magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.

senses.d: To exaggerate; as, to magnify a loss or a difficulty.

Magnify.etym: [OE. magnifien, F. magnifier, L. magnificare. See Magnific.]

senses.d: To have the power of causing objects to appear larger than they really are; to increase the apparent dimensions of objects; as, some lenses magnify but little.
To have effect; to be of importance or significance.
A kind of baboon; the wanderoo.
An unmarried woman; usually, a young unmarried woman; esp., a girl; a virgin; a maiden.
q: Would I had died a maid, And never seen thee, never borne thee son.
Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? Yet my people have forgotten me.

senses.d: A man who has not had sexual intercourse.
q: Christ was a maid and shapen as a man.

senses.d: A female servant.
q: Spinning amongst her maids.

senses.d: The female of a ray or skate, esp. of the gray skate (Raia batis), and of the thornback (R. clavata).
An unmarried woman; a girl or woman who has not experienced sexual intercourse; a virgin; a maid.
q: She employed the residue of her life to repairing of highways, building of bridges, and endowing of maidens.
A maiden of our century, yet most meek.

senses.d: A female servant.
An instrument resembling the guillotine, formerly used in Scotland for beheading criminals.
A machine for washing linen.

Maiden.etym: [OE. maiden, meiden, AS. mægden, dim. of AS. mæg�, fr. mago son, servant; akin to G. magd, mädchen, maid, OHG. magad, Icel. mögr son, Goth. magus boy, child, magaps virgin, and perh. to Zend. magu youth. Cf. Maid a virgin.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a maiden, or to maidens; suitable to, or characteristic of, a virgin; as, maiden innocence.
q: Have you no modesty, no maiden shame ?

senses.d: Never having been married; not having had sexual intercourse; virgin; — said usually of the woman, but sometimes of the man; as, a maiden aunt.
Fresh; innocent; unpolluted; pure; hitherto unused.
q: Full bravely hast thou fleshed Thy maiden sword.

senses.d: Used of a fortress, signifying that it has never been captured, or violated.
To act coyly like a maiden; — with it as an indefinite object.
q: For had I maiden'd it, as many use. Loath for to grant, but loather to refuse.

senses.d: A female servant.
A spot.
A small piece of money; especially, an English silver half-penny of the time of Henry V.
Rent; tribute.

Mail.etym: [F. maille, OF. also maaille, LL. medalia. See Medal.]

senses.d: A flexible fabric made of metal rings interlinked. It was used especially for defensive armor.
Hence generally, armor, or any defensive covering.
A contrivance of interlinked rings, for rubbing off the loose hemp on lines and white cordage.
Any hard protective covering of an animal, as the scales and plates of reptiles, shell of a lobster, etc.
q: We . . . strip the lobster of his scarlet mail.

Mail.etym: [OE. maile, maille, F. maille a ring of mail, mesh, network, a coat of mail, fr. L. macula spot, a mesh of a net. Cf. Macle, Macula, Mascle.]

senses.d: To arm with mail.
To pinion.
A bag; a wallet.

The bag or bags with the letters, papers, or other matter contained therein, conveyed under public authority from one post office to another; the whole system of appliances used by government in the conveyance and delivery of mail matter.
q: There is a mail come in to-day, with letters dated Hague.

senses.d: That which comes in the mail; letters, etc., received through the post office.
A trunk, box, or bag, in which clothing, etc., may be carried.

Mail.etym: [OE. male bag, OF. male, F. malle bag, trunk, mail, OHG. malaha, malha, wallet; akin to D. maal, male; cf. Gael. & Ir. mala, Gr. μολγόσ hide, skin.]

senses.d: To deliver into the custody of the postoffice officials, or place in a government letter box, for transmission by mail; to post; as, to mail a letter.
To deprive of the use of a limb, so as to render a person in fighting less able either to defend himself or to annoy his adversary.
q: By the ancient law of England he that maimed any man whereby he lost any part of his body, was sentenced to lose the like part.

senses.d: To mutilate; to cripple; to injure; to disable; to impair.
q: My late maimed limbs lack wonted might.
You maimed the jurisdiction of all bishops.

Maim.etym: [OE. maimen, OF. mahaignier, mehaignier, meshaignier, cf. It. magagnare, LL. mahemiare, mahennare; perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Armor. mac'haña to mutilate, māc'ha to crowd, press; or cf. OHG. mangōn to lack, perh. akin to E. mangle to lacerate. Cf. Mayhem.]

senses.d: The privation of the use of a limb or member of the body, by which one is rendered less able to defend himself or to annoy his adversary.
The privation of any necessary part; a crippling; mutilation; injury; deprivation of something essential. See Mayhem.
q: Surely there is more cause to fear lest the want there of be a maim than the use of it a blemish.
A noble author esteems it to be a maim in history that the acts of Parliament should not be recited.

senses.d: The principal sail in a ship or other vessel.
q: hoised up the mainsail to the wind.

senses.d: To hold or keep in any particular state or condition; to support; to sustain; to uphold; to keep up; not to suffer to fail or decline; as, to maintain a certain degree of heat in a furnace; to maintain a fence or a railroad; to maintain the digestive process or powers of the stomach; to maintain the fertility of soil; to maintain present reputation.
To keep possession of; to hold and defend; not to surrender or relinquish.
q: God values . . . every one as he maintains his post.

senses.d: To continue; not to suffer to cease or fail.
q: Maintain talk with the duke.

senses.d: To bear the expense of; to support; to keep up; to supply with what is needed.
q: Glad, by his labor, to maintain his life.
What maintains one vice would bring up two children.

senses.d: To affirm; to support or defend by argument.
q: It is hard to maintain the truth, but much harder to be maintained by it.

Maintain.syn: To assert; vindicate; allege. See Assert.
Maintain.etym: [OE. maintenen, F. maintenir, properly, to hold by the hand; main hand (L. manus) + F. tenir to hold (L. tenere). See Manual, and Tenable.]

senses.d: The act of maintaining; sustenance; support; defense; vindication.
q: Whatsoever is granted to the church for God's honor and the maintenance of his service, is granted to God.

senses.d: That which maintains or supports; means of sustenance; supply of necessaries and conveniences.
q: Those of better fortune not making learning their maintenance.

senses.d: An officious or unlawful intermeddling in a cause depending between others, by assisting either party with money or means to carry it on. See Champerty.

The dignity and authority of sovereign power; quality or state which inspires awe or reverence; grandeur; exalted dignity, whether proceeding from rank, character, or bearing; imposing loftiness; stateliness; — usually applied to the rank and dignity of sovereigns.
q: The Lord reigneth; he is clothed with majesty.
No sovereign has ever represented the majesty of a great state with more dignity and grace.

senses.d: Hence, used with the possessive pronoun, the title of an emperor, king or queen; — in this sense taking a plural; as, their majesties attended the concert.
q: In all the public writs which he [Emperor Charles V.] now issued as King of Spain, he assumed the title of Majesty, and required it from his subjects as a mark of respect. Before that time all the monarchs of Europe were satisfied with the appellation of Highness or Grace.

senses.d: Dignity; elevation of manner or style.

Majesty.etym: [OE. magestee, F. majesté, L. majestas, fr. an old compar. of magnus great. See Major, Master.]

senses.d: A companion; a mate; often, a husband or a wife.
q: For in this world no woman is Worthy to be my make.

senses.d: To cause to exist; to bring into being; to form; to produce; to frame; to fashion; to create.
q: He . . . fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf.

senses.d: To produce, as something artificial, unnatural, or false; — often with up; as, to make up a story.
q: And Art, with her contending, doth aspire To excel the natural with made delights.

senses.d: To bring about; to bring forward; to be the cause or agent of; to effect, do, perform, or execute; — often used with a noun to form a phrase equivalent to the simple verb that corresponds to such noun; as, to make complaint, for to complain; to make record of, for to record; to make abode, for to abide, etc.
q: Call for Samson, that he may make us sport.
Wealth maketh many friends.
I will neither plead my age nor sickness in excuse of the faults which I have made.

senses.d: To execute with the requisite formalities; as, to make a bill, note, will, deed, etc.
To gain, as the result of one's efforts; to get, as profit; to make acquisition of; to have accrue or happen to one; as, to make a large profit; to make an error; to make a loss; to make money.
q: He accuseth Neptune unjustly who makes shipwreck a second time.

senses.d: To find, as the result of calculation or computation; to ascertain by enumeration; to find the number or amount of, by reckoning, weighing, measurement, and the like; as, he made the distance of; to travel over; as, the ship makes ten knots an hour; he made the distance in one day.
To put in a desired or desirable condition; to cause to thrive.
q: Who makes or ruins with a smile or frown.

senses.d: To cause to be or become; to put into a given state verb, or adjective; to constitute; as, to make known; to make public; to make fast.
q: Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?
See, I have made thee a god to Pharaoh.

senses.d: To cause to appear to be; to constitute subjectively; to esteem, suppose, or represent.
q: He is not that goose and ass that Valla would make him.

senses.d: To require; to constrain; to compel; to force; to cause; to occasion; — followed by a noun or pronoun and infinitive.
q: I will make them hear my words.
They should be made to rise at their early hour.

senses.d: To become; to be, or to be capable of being, changed or fashioned into; to do the part or office of; to furnish the material for; as, he will make a good musician; sweet cider makes sour vinegar; wool makes warm clothing.
q: And old cloak makes a new jerkin.

senses.d: To compose, as parts, ingredients, or materials; to constitute; to form; to amount to.
q: The heaven, the air, the earth, and boundless sea, Make but one temple for the Deity.

Make.etym: [OE. maken, makien, AS. macian; akin to OS. mak�n, OFries. makia, D. maken, G. machen, OHG. mahh�n to join, fit, prepare, make, Dan. mage. Cf. Match an equal.]

senses.d: To act in a certain manner; to have to do; to manage; to interfere; to be active; — often in the phrase to meddle or make.
q: A scurvy, jack-a-nape priest to meddle or make.

senses.d: To proceed; to tend; to move; to go; as, he made toward home; the tiger made at the sportsmen.
To tend; to contribute; to have effect; — with for or against; as, it makes for his advantage.
q: Follow after the things which make for peace.
Considerations infinite Do make against it.

senses.d: To increase; to augment; to accrue.
To compose verses; to write poetry; to versify.
q: To solace him some time, as I do when I make.

senses.d: Structure, texture, constitution of parts; construction; shape; form.
q: It our perfection of so frail a make As every plot can undermine and shake?

senses.d: One who makes, forms, or molds; a manufacturer; specifically, the Creator.
q: The universal Maker we may praise.

senses.d: The person who makes a promissory note.
One who writes verses; a poet.
The act of one who makes; workmanship; fabrication; construction; as, this is cloth of your own making; the making of peace or war was in his power.
Composition, or structure.
a poem.
That which establishes or places in a desirable state or condition; the material of which something may be made; as, early misfortune was the making of him.
External appearance; from.
Evil; wicked; bad.
Same as Mail, a bag.
Of or pertaining to the sex that begets or procreates young, or (in a wider sense) to the sex that produces spermatozoa, by which the ova are fertilized; not female; as, male organs.
Capable of producing fertilization, but not of bearing fruit; — said of stamens and antheridia, and of the plants, or parts of plants, which bear them.
Suitable to the male sex; characteristic or suggestive of a male; masculine; as, male courage.
Consisting of males; as, a male choir.
Adapted for entering another corresponding piece (the female piece) which is hollow and which it fits; as, a male gauge, for gauging the size or shape of a hole; a male screw, etc.

Male.etym: [F. mâle, OF. masle, mascle, fr. L. masculus male, masculine, dim. of mas a male; possibly akin to E. man. Cf. Masculine, Marry, v. t.]

senses.d: An animal of the male sex.
A plant bearing only staminate flowers.
An evil doer; one who commits a crime; one subject to public prosecution and punishment; a criminal.
One who does wrong by injuring another, although not a criminal.

Malefactor.syn: Evil doer; criminal; culprit; felon; convict.
Malefactor.etym: [L., fr. malefacere to do evil; male ill, evil + facere to do. See Malice, and Fact.]

senses.d: Enmity of heart; malevolence; ill will; a spirit delighting in harm or misfortune to another; a disposition to injure another; a malignant design of evil.
q: Envy, hatred, and malice are three distinct passions of the mind.

senses.d: Any wicked or mischievous intention of the mind; a depraved inclination to mischief; an intention to vex, annoy, or injure another person, or to do a wrongful act without just cause or cause or excuse; a wanton disregard of the rights or safety of others; willfulness.
q: Proud tyrants who maliciously destroy And ride o'er ruins with malignant joy.
in some connections, malignity seems rather more pertinently applied to a radical depravity of nature, and malignancy to indications of this depravity, in temper and conduct in particular instances.

Malice.syn: Spite; ill will; malevolence; grudge; pique; bitterness; animosity; malignity; maliciousness; rancor; virulence.
Malice.etym: [F. malice, fr. L. malitia, from malus bad, ill, evil, prob. orig., dirty, black; cf. Gr. μέλασ black, Skr. mala dirt. Cf. Mauger.]

senses.d: To regard with extreme ill will.
Indulging or exercising malice; harboring ill will or enmity.
q: I grant him bloody, . . . Sudden, malicious, smacking of every sin That has a name.

senses.d: Proceeding from hatred or ill will; dictated by malice; as, a malicious report; malicious mischief.
With wicked or mischievous intentions or motives; wrongful and done intentionally without just cause or excuse; as, a malicious act.

Malicious.syn: Ill-disposed; evil-minded; mischievous; envious; malevolent; invidious; spiteful; bitter; malignant; rancorous; malign.
Malicious.etym: [Of. malicius, F. malicieux, fr. L. malitiosus. See Malice.]

senses.d: The state or quality of being malignant; disposition to do evil; virulent enmity; malignancy; malice; spite.
Virulence; deadly quality.
q: His physicians discerned an invincible malignity in his disease.

senses.d: Extreme evilness of nature or influence; perniciousness; heinousness; as, the malignity of fraud.
A genus of plants (Malva) having mucilaginous qualities. See Malvaceous.

Mallow.etym: [OE. malwe, AS. mealwe, fr. L. malva, akin to Gr. μαλάχη; cf. μαλάσσειν to soften, μαλακόσ soft. Named either from its softening or relaxing properties, or from its soft downy leaves. Cf. Mauve, Malachite.]

senses.d: Riches; wealth; the god of riches; riches, personified.
q: Ye can not serve God and Mammon.

Mammon.etym: [L. mammona, Gr. � riches, Syr. mam�nā; cf. Heb. matm�n a hiding place, subterranean storehouse, treasury, fr. tāman to hide.]

senses.d: A human being; — opposed to beast.
q: These men went about wide, and man found they none, But fair country, and wild beast many one.
The king is but a man, as I am; the violet smells to him as it doth to me.

senses.d: Especially: An adult male person; a grown-up male person, as distinguished from a woman or a child.
q: When I became a man, I put away childish things.
Ceneus, a woman once, and once a man.

senses.d: The human race; mankind.
q: And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness, and let them have dominion.
The proper study of mankind is man.

senses.d: The male portion of the human race.
q: Woman has, in general, much stronger propensity than man to the discharge of parental duties.

senses.d: One possessing in a high degree the distinctive qualities of manhood; one having manly excellence of any kind.
q: This was the noblest Roman of them all . . . the elements So mixed in him that Nature might stand up And say to all the world “This was a man!”

senses.d: An adult male servant; also, a vassal; a subject.
q: Like master, like man.
The vassal, or tenant, kneeling, ungirt, uncovered, and holding up his hands between those of his lord, professed that he did become his man from that day forth, of life, limb, and earthly honor.

senses.d: A term of familiar address often implying on the part of the speaker some degree of authority, impatience, or haste; as, Come, man, we 've no time to lose!
A married man; a husband; — correlative to wife.
q: I pronounce that they are man and wife.
every wife ought to answer for her man.

senses.d: One, or any one, indefinitely; — a modified survival of the Saxon use of man, or mon, as an indefinite pronoun.
q: A man can not make him laugh.
A man would expect to find some antiquities; but all they have to show of this nature is an old rostrum of a Roman ship.

senses.d: One of the piece with which certain games, as chess or draughts, are played.

Man.etym: [AS. mann, man, monn, mon; akin to OS., D., & OHG. man, G. mann, Icel. maðr, for mannr, Dan. Mand, Sw. man, Goth. manna, Skr. manu, manus, and perh. to Skr. man to think, and E. mind. √104. Cf. Minx a pert girl.]

senses.d: To supply with men; to furnish with a sufficient force or complement of men, as for management, service, defense, or the like; to guard; as, to man a ship, boat, or fort.
q: See how the surly Warwick mans the wall !
They man their boats, and all their young men arm.

senses.d: To furnish with strength for action; to prepare for efficiency; to fortify.
To tame, as a hawk.
To furnish with a servant or servants.
To wait on as a manservant.

A low plant (Mandragora officinarum) of the Nightshade family, having a fleshy root, often forked, and supposed to resemble a man. It was therefore supposed to have animal life, and to cry out when pulled up. All parts of the plant are strongly narcotic. It is found in the Mediterranean region.
q: And shrieks like mandrakes, torn out of the earth, That living mortals, hearing them, run mad.

senses.d: The May apple (Podophyllum peltatum). See May apple under May, and Podophyllum.

Mandrake.etym: [AS. mandragora, L. mandragoras, fr. Gr. μανδραγόρασ: cf. F. mandragore.]

senses.d: A Hebrew weight for gold or silver, being one hundred shekels of gold and sixty shekels of silver.
The scab or itch in cattle, dogs, and other beasts.
A trough or open box in which fodder is placed for horses or cattle to eat.
The fore part of the deck, having a bulkhead athwart ships high enough to prevent water which enters the hawse holes from running over it.

Manger.etym: [F. mangeoire, fr. manger to eat, fr. L. manducare, fr. mandere to chew. Cf. Mandible, Manducate.]

senses.d: Evident to the senses, esp. to the sight; apparent; distinctly perceived; hence, obvious to the understanding; apparent to the mind; easily apprehensible; plain; not obscure or hidden.
q: Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight.
That which may be known of God is manifest in them.
Thus manifest to sight the god appeared.

senses.d: Detected; convicted; — with of.
q: Calistho there stood manifest of shame.
So clear, so shining, and so evident, That it will glimmer through a blind man's eye.
Entertained with solitude, Where obvious duty erewhile appeared unsought.
I saw, I saw him manifest in view, His voice, his figure, and his gesture knew.

Manifest.syn: Open; clear; apparent; evident; visible; conspicuous; plain; obvious.
Manifest.etym: [F. manifeste, L. manifestus, lit., struck by the hand, hence, palpable; manus hand + fendere (in comp.) to strike. See Manual, and Defend.]

senses.d: A public declaration; an open statement; a manifesto. See Manifesto.
A list or invoice of a ship's cargo, containing a description by marks, numbers, etc., of each package of goods, to be exhibited at the customhouse.

Manifest.etym: [Cf. F. manifeste. See Manifest, a., and cf. Manifesto.]

senses.d: To show plainly; to make to appear distinctly, — usually to the mind; to put beyond question or doubt; to display; to exhibit.
q: There is nothing hid which shall not be manifested.
Thy life did manifest thou lovedst me not.

senses.d: To exhibit the manifests or prepared invoices of; to declare at the customhouse.

Manifest.syn: To reveal; declare; evince; make known; disclose; discover; display.

senses.d: The act of manifesting or disclosing, or the state of being manifested; discovery to the eye or to the understanding; also, that which manifests; exhibition; display; revelation; as, the manifestation of God's power in creation.
q: The secret manner in which acts of mercy ought to be performed, requires this public manifestation of them at the great day.

senses.d: In a manifest manner.
Various in kind or quality; many in number; numerous; multiplied; complicated.
q: O Lord, how manifold are thy works!
I know your manifold transgressions.

senses.d: Exhibited at divers times or in various ways; — used to qualify nouns in the singular number.
A copy of a writing made by the manifold process.
A cylindrical pipe fitting, having a number of lateral outlets, for connecting one pipe with several others.
The third stomach of a ruminant animal.
To take copies of by the process of manifold writing; as, to manifold a letter.
The human race; man, taken collectively.
q: The proper study of mankind is man.

senses.d: Men, as distinguished from women; the male portion of human race.
Human feelings; humanity.

Mankind.etym: [AS. mancynn. See Kin kindred, Kind, n.]

senses.d: Manlike; not womanly; masculine; bold; cruel.
q: Are women grown so mankind? Must they be wooing?
Be not too mankind against your wife.

senses.d: The food supplied to the Israelites in their journey through the wilderness of Arabia; hence, divinely supplied food.
A name given to lichens of the genus Lecanora, sometimes blown into heaps in the deserts of Arabia and Africa, and gathered and used as food.

A sweetish exudation in the form of pale yellow friable flakes, coming from several trees and shrubs and used in medicine as a gentle laxative, as the secretion of Fraxinus Ornus, and F. rotundifolia, the manna ashes of Southern Europe.

Manna.etym: [L., fr. Gr. μάννα, Heb. mān; cf. Ar. mann, properly, gift (of heaven).]

senses.d: Mode of action; way of performing or effecting anything; method; style; form; fashion.
q: The nations which thou hast removed, and placed in the cities of Samaria, know not the manner of the God of the land.
The temptations of prosperity insinuate themselves after a gentle, but very powerful, manner.

senses.d: Characteristic mode of acting, conducting, carrying one's self, or the like; bearing; habitual style.
Customary method of acting; habit.
q: Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them.
Air and manner are more expressive than words.

senses.d: Carriage; behavior; deportment; also, becoming behavior; well-bred carriage and address.
q: Good manners are made up of petty sacrifices.

senses.d: The style of writing or thought of an author; characteristic peculiarity of an artist.
Certain degree or measure; as, it is in a manner done already.
q: The bread is in a manner common.

senses.d: Sort; kind; style; — in this application sometimes having the sense of a plural, sorts or kinds.
q: Ye tithe mint, and rue, and all manner of herbs.
I bid thee say, What manner of man art thou?

Manner.syn: Method; mode; custom; habit; fashion; air; look; mien; aspect; appearance. See Method.
Manner.etym: [OE. manere, F. manière, from OF. manier, adj., manual, skillful, handy, fr. (assumed) LL. manarius, for L. manuarius belonging to the hand, fr. manus the hand. See Manual.]

senses.d: A male servant.
A dwelling place, — whether a part or whole of a house or other shelter.
q: In my Father's house are many mansions.
These poets near our princes sleep, And in one grave their mansions keep.

senses.d: The house of the lord of a manor; a manor house; hence: Any house of considerable size or pretension.
A twelfth part of the heavens; a house. See 1st House, 8.
The place in the heavens occupied each day by the moon in its monthly revolution.
q: The eight and twenty mansions That longen to the moon.

Mansion.etym: [OF. mansion, F. maison, fr. L. mansio a staying, remaining, a dwelling, habitation, fr. manere, mansum, to stay, dwell; akin to Gr. �. Cf. Manse, Manor, Menagerie, Menial, Permanent.]

senses.d: To dwell; to reside.
One who kills a human being; one who commits manslaughter.
A loose garment to be worn over other garments; an enveloping robe; a cloak. Hence, figuratively, a covering or concealing envelope.
q: children are clothed with mantles of satin.
The green mantle of the standing pool.
Now Nature hangs her mantle green On every blooming tree.

senses.d: Same as Mantling.
The external fold, or folds, of the soft, exterior membrane of the body of a mollusk. It usually forms a cavity inclosing the gills. See Illusts. of Buccinum, and Byssus.
A mantel. See Mantel.
The outer wall and casing of a blast furnace, above the hearth.
A penstock for a water wheel.

Mantle.etym: [OE. mantel, OF. mantel, F. manteau, fr. L. mantellum, mantelum, a cloth, napkin, cloak, mantle (cf. mantele, mantile, towel, napkin); prob. from manus hand + the root of tela cloth. See Manual, Textile, and cf. Mandil, Mantel, Mantilla.]

senses.d: To cover or envelop, as with a mantle; to cloak; to hide; to disguise.
To unfold and spread out the wings, like a mantle; — said of hawks. Also used figuratively.
q: Ne is there hawk which mantleth on her perch.
Or tend his sparhawk mantling in her mew.
My frail fancy fed with full delight. Doth bathe in bliss, and mantleth most at ease.

senses.d: To spread out; — said of wings.
q: The swan, with arched neck Between her white wings mantling proudly, rows.

senses.d: To spread over the surface as a covering; to overspread; as, the scum mantled on the pool.
q: Though mantled in her cheek the blood.

senses.d: To gather, assume, or take on, a covering, as froth, scum, etc.
q: There is a sort of men whose visages Do cream and mantle like a standing pond.
Nor bowl of wassail mantle warm.

senses.d: A retinue of servants; a household.
Consisting of a great number; numerous; not few.
q: Thou shalt be a father of many nations.
Not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called.

Many.syn: Numerous; multiplied; frequent; manifold; various; divers; sundry.
Many.etym: [OE. mani, moni, AS. manig, mænig, monig; akin to D. menig, OS. & OHG. manag, G. manch, Dan. mange, Sw. månge, Goth. manags, OSlav. mnog', Russ. mnogii; cf. Icel. margr, Prov. E. mort. √103.]

senses.d: The populace; the common people; the majority of people, or of a community.
q: After him the rascal many ran.

senses.d: A large or considerable number.
q: A many of our bodies shall no doubt Find native graves.
Seeing a great many in rich gowns.
It will be concluded by manythat he lived like an honest man.
He is liable to a great many inconveniences.

Many.etym: [AS. menigeo, menigo, menio, multitude; akin to G. menge, OHG. managī, menigī, Goth. managei. See Many, a.]

senses.d: A small lake. See Mere.
To make defective; to do injury to, esp. by cutting off or defacing a part; to impair; to disfigure; to deface.
q: I pray you mar no more trees with wiring love songs in their barks.
But mirth is marred, and the good cheer is lost.
Ire, envy, and despair Which marred all his borrowed visage.

senses.d: To spoil; to ruin.

Mar.etym: [OE. marren, merren, AS. merran, myrran (in comp.), to obstruct, impede, dissipate; akin to OS. merrian, OHG. marrjan, merran; cf. D. marren, meeren, to moor a ship, Icel. merja to bruise, crush, and Goth. marzjan to offend. Cf. Moor, v.]

senses.d: A mark or blemish made by bruising, scratching, or the like; a disfigurement.
The principal or ruling evil spirit.
A female demon who torments people in sleep by crouching on their chests or stomachs, or by causing terrifying visions.

Mara.etym: [Icel. mara nightmare, an ogress. See Nightmare.]

senses.d: The Patagonian cavy (Dolichotis Patagonicus).

A massive, compact limestone; a variety of calcite, capable of being polished and used for architectural and ornamental purposes. The color varies from white to black, being sometimes yellow, red, and green, and frequently beautifully veined or clouded. The name is also given to other rocks of like use and appearance, as serpentine or verd antique marble, and less properly to polished porphyry, granite, etc.
A thing made of, or resembling, marble, as a work of art, or record, in marble; or, in the plural, a collection of such works; as, the Arundel or Arundelian marbles; the Elgin marbles.
A little ball of marble, or of some other hard substance, used as a plaything by children; or, in the plural, a child's game played with marbles.

Marble.etym: [OE. marbel, marbre, F. marbre, L. marmor, fr. Gr. μάρμαροσ, fr. μαρμαίρειν to sparkle, flash. Cf. Marmoreal.]

senses.d: Made of, or resembling, marble; as, a marble mantel; marble paper.
Cold; hard; unfeeling; as, a marble breast or heart.
To stain or vein like marble; to variegate in color; as, to marble the edges of a book, or the surface of paper.
The third month of the year, containing thirty-one days.
q: The stormy March is come at last, With wind, and cloud, and changing skies.

March.etym: [L. Martius mensis Mars'month fr. Martius belonging to Mars, the god of war: cf. F. mars. Cf. Martial.]

senses.d: A territorial border or frontier; a region adjacent to a boundary line; a confine; — used chiefly in the plural, and in English history applied especially to the border land on the frontiers between England and Scotland, and England and Wales.
q: Geneva is situated in the marches of several dominions — France, Savoy, and Switzerland.
Lords of waste marches, kings of desolate isles.

March.etym: [OE. marche, F. marche; of German origin; cf. OHG. marcha, G. mark, akin to OS. marka, AS. mearc, Goth. marka, L. margo edge, border, margin, and possibly to E. mark a sign. √106. Cf. Margin, Margrave, Marque, Marquis.]

senses.d: To border; to be contiguous; to lie side by side.
q: That was in a strange land Which marcheth upon Chimerie.

senses.d: To move with regular steps, as a soldier; to walk in a grave, deliberate, or stately manner; to advance steadily.
To proceed by walking in a body or in military order; as, the German army marched into France.

March.etym: [F. marcher, in OF. also, to tread, prob. fr. L. marcus hammer. Cf. Mortar.]

senses.d: To cause to move with regular steps in the manner of a soldier; to cause to move in military array, or in a body, as troops; to cause to advance in a steady, regular, or stately manner; to cause to go by peremptory command, or by force.
q: March them again in fair array.

senses.d: The act of marching; a movement of soldiers from one stopping place to another; military progress; advance of troops.
q: These troops came to the army harassed with a long and wearisome march.

senses.d: Hence: Measured and regular advance or movement, like that of soldiers moving in order; stately or deliberate walk; steady onward movement.
q: With solemn march Goes slow and stately by them.
This happens merely because men will not bide their time, but will insist on precipitating the march of affairs.

senses.d: The distance passed over in marching; as, an hour's march; a march of twenty miles.
A piece of music designed or fitted to accompany and guide the movement of troops; a piece of music in the march form.
q: The drums presently striking up a march.

senses.d: One whose occupation is to assist in navigating ships; a seaman or sailor.
Low, wet ground; a marsh; a fen; a bog; a moor.

Marish.etym: [Cf. F. marais, LL. marascus. See Marsh.]

senses.d: Moory; fenny; boggy.
Growing in marshes.
A license of reprisals. See Marque.
An old weight and coin. See Marc.
The unit of monetary account of the German Empire, equal to 23.8 cents of United States money; the equivalent of one hundred pfennigs. Also, a silver coin of this value.

A visible sign or impression made or left upon anything; esp., a line, point, stamp, figure, or the like, drawn or impressed, so as to attract the attention and convey some information or intimation; a token; a trace.
q: The Lord set a mark upon Cain, lest any finding him should kill him.

senses.d: A character or device put on an article of merchandise by the maker to show by whom it was made; a trade-mark.
q: The mark of the artisan is found upon the most ancient fabrics that have come to light.

senses.d: A fixed object serving for guidance, as of a ship, a traveler, a surveyor, etc.; as, a seamark, a landmark.
A trace, dot, line, imprint, or discoloration, although not regarded as a token or sign; a scratch, scar, stain, etc.; as, this pencil makes a fine mark.
q: I have some marks of yours upon my pate.

senses.d: An evidence of presence, agency, or influence; a significative token; a symptom; a trace; specifically, a permanent impression of one's activity or character.
q: The confusion of tongues was a mark of separation.

senses.d: That toward which a missile is directed; a thing aimed at; what one seeks to hit or reach.
q: France was a fairer mark to shoot at than Ireland.
Whate'er the motive, pleasure is the mark.

senses.d: Attention, regard, or respect.
q: As much in mock as mark.

senses.d: Limit or standard of action or fact; as, to be within the mark; to come up to the mark.
Badge or sign of honor, rank, or official station.
q: In the official marks invested, you Anon do meet the Senate.

senses.d: Preëminence; high position; as, patricians of mark; a fellow of no mark.
A characteristic or essential attribute; a differential.
A number or other character used in registering; as, examination marks; a mark for tardiness.

Mark.syn: Impress; impression; stamp; print; trace; vestige; track; characteristic; evidence; proof; token; badge; indication; symptom.
Mark.etym: [OE. marke, merke, AS. mearc; akin to D. merk, MHG. marc, G. marke, Icel. mark, Dan. mærke; cf. Lith. margas party-colored. √106, 273. Cf. Remark.]

senses.d: To put a mark upon; to affix a significant mark to; to make recognizable by a mark; as, to mark a box or bale of merchandise; to mark clothing.
To be a mark upon; to designate; to indicate; — used literally and figuratively; as, this monument marks the spot where Wolfe died; his courage and energy marked him for a leader.
To leave a trace, scratch, scar, or other mark, upon, or any evidence of action; as, a pencil marks paper; his hobnails marked the floor.
To keep account of; to enumerate and register; as, to mark the points in a game of billiards or cards.
To notice or observe; to give attention to; to take note of; to remark; to heed; to regard.

Mark.syn: To note; remark; notice; observe; regard; heed; show; evince; indicate; point out; betoken; denote; characterize; stamp; imprint; impress; brand.
Mark.etym: [OE. marken, merken, AS. mearcian, from mearc. See Mark the sign.]

senses.d: To take particular notice; to observe critically; to note; to remark.
q: Mark, I pray you, and see how this man seeketh mischief.

senses.d: Designated or distinguished by, or as by, a mark; hence; noticeable; conspicuous; as, a marked card; a marked coin; a marked instance.

A meeting together of people, at a stated time and place, for the purpose of traffic (as in cattle, provisions, wares, etc.) by private purchase and sale, and not by auction; as, a market is held in the town every week.
q: He is wit's peddler; and retails his wares At wakes, and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs.
Three women and a goose make a market.

senses.d: A public place (as an open space in a town) or a large building, where a market is held; a market place or market house; esp., a place where provisions are sold.
q: There is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool.

senses.d: An opportunity for selling anything; demand, as shown by price offered or obtainable; a town, region, or country, where the demand exists; as, to find a market for one's wares; there is no market for woolen cloths in that region; India is a market for English goods.
q: There is a third thing to be considered: how a market can be created for produce, or how production can be limited to the capacities of the market.

senses.d: Exchange, or purchase and sale; traffic; as, a dull market; a slow market.
The price for which a thing is sold in a market; market price. Hence: Value; worth.
q: What is a man If his chief good and market of his time Be but to sleep and feed ?

senses.d: The privelege granted to a town of having a public market.

Market.etym: [Akin to D. markt, OHG. markāt, merkāt, G. markt; all fr.L. mercatus trade, market place, fr. mercari, p. p. mercatus, to trade, traffic, merx, mercis, ware, merchandise, prob. akin to merere to deserve, gain, acquire: cf. F. marché. See Merit, and cf. Merchant, Mart.]

senses.d: To deal in a market; to buy or sell; to make bargains for provisions or goods.
To expose for sale in a market; to traffic in; to sell in a market, and in an extended sense, to sell in any manner; as, most of the farmes have marketed their crops.
q: Industrious merchants meet, and market there The world's collected wealth.

senses.d: The act of marrying, or the state of being married; legal union of a man and a woman for life, as husband and wife; wedlock; matrimony.
q: Marriage is honorable in all.

senses.d: The marriage vow or contract.
A feast made on the occasion of a marriage.
q: The kingdom of heaven is like unto a certain king which made a marriage for his son.

senses.d: Any intimate or close union.

Marriage.etym: [OE. mariage, F. mariage. See Marry, v. t.]

senses.d: In bézique, penuchle, and similar games at cards, the combination of a king and queen of the same suit. If of the trump suit, it is called a royal marriage.
Being in the state of matrimony; wedded; as, a married man or woman.
Of or pertaining to marriage; connubial; as, the married state.
The tissue which fills the cavities of most bones; the medulla. In the larger cavities it is commonly very fatty, but in the smaller cavities it is much less fatty, and red or reddish in color.
The essence; the best part.
q: It takes from our achievements . . . The pith and marrow of our attribute.

senses.d: One of a pair; a match; a companion; an intimate associate.
q: Chopping and changing I can not commend, With thief or his marrow, for fear of ill end.

Marrow.etym: [OE. marou, mary, maruh, AS. mearg, mearh; akin to OS. marg, D. merg, G. Mark, OHG. marg, marag, Icel. mergr, Sw. merg, Dan. marv, Skr. majjan; cf. Skr. majj to sink, L. mergere. √274 Cf. Merge.]

senses.d: To fill with, or as with, marrow or fat; to glut.
To unite in wedlock or matrimony; to perform the ceremony of joining, as a man and a woman, for life; to constitute (a man and a woman) husband and wife according to the laws or customs of the place.
q: Tell him that he shall marry the couple himself.

senses.d: To join according to law, (a man) to a woman as his wife, or (a woman) to a man as her husband. See the Note to def. 4.
q: A woman who had been married to her twenty-fifth husband, and being now a widow, was prohibited to marry.

senses.d: To dispose of in wedlock; to give away as wife.
q: Mæcenas took the liberty to tell him that he must either marry his daughter to Agrippa, or take away his life.

senses.d: To take for husband or wife. See the Note below.
q: They got him . . . to declare in writing, that the last king told him he was never married to his mother.

senses.d: Figuratively, to unite in the closest and most endearing relation.
q: Turn, O backsliding children, saith the Lord; for I am married unto you.

Marry.etym: [OE. marien, F. marier, L. maritare, fr. maritus husband, fr. mas, maris, a male. See Male, and cf. Maritral.]

senses.d: To enter into the conjugal or connubial state; to take a husband or a wife.
q: I will, therefore, that the younger women marry.

senses.d: Indeed ! in truth ! — a term of asseveration said to have been derived from the practice of swearing by the Virgin Mary.
The god of war and husbandry.

One of the planets of the solar system, the fourth in order from the sun, or the next beyond the earth, having a diameter of about 4,200 miles, a period of 687 days, and a mean distance of 141,000,000 miles. It is conspicuous for the redness of its light.
The metallic element iron, the symbol of which ♂ was the same as that of the planet Mars.

Mars.etym: [L. Mars, gen. Martis, archaic Mavors, gen. Mavortis.]

senses.d: A market.
q: Where has commerce such a mart . . . as London ?

senses.d: A bargain.
To buy or sell in, or as in, a mart.
q: To sell and mart your officer for gold To undeservers.

senses.d: To traffic.
The god Mars.
Battle; contest.
One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; one who is put to death for his religion; as, Stephen was the first Christian martyr.
q: To be a martyr, signifies only to witness the truth of Christ; but the witnessing of the truth was then so generally attended with persecution, that martyrdom now signifies not only to witness, but to witness by death.

senses.d: Hence, one who sacrifices his life, his station, or what is of great value to him, for the sake of principle, or to sustain a cause.
q: Then if thou fall'st, O Cromwell, Thou fall'st a blessed martyr !

Martyr.etym: [AS., from L. martyr, Gr. μάρτυρ, μάρτυσ, prop., a witness; cf. Skr. smṛ to remember, E. memory.]

senses.d: To put to death for adhering to some belief, esp. Christianity; to sacrifice on account of faith or profession.
To persecute; to torment; to torture.
q: The lovely Amoret, whose gentle heart Thou martyrest with sorrow and with smart.
Racked with sciatics, martyred with the stone.

senses.d: That which causes wonder; a prodigy; a miracle.
q: I will do marvels such as have not been done.
Nature's sweet marvel undefiled.

senses.d: Wonder.

Marvel.etym: [OE. mervaile, F. merveille, fr. L. mirabilia wonderful things, pl., fr. mirabilis wonderful, fr. mirari to wonder or marvel at. See Admire, Smile, and cf. Miracle.]

senses.d: To be struck with surprise, astonishment, or wonder; to wonder.
q: Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you.

senses.d: To marvel at.
To cause to marvel, or be surprised; — used impersonally.
q: But much now me marveleth.

senses.d: Marrow.
A mesh.

A mass of mixed ingredients reduced to a soft pulpy state by beating or pressure; a mass of anything in a soft pulpy state. Specifically (Brewing), ground or bruised malt, or meal of rye, wheat, corn, or other grain (or a mixture of malt and meal) steeped and stirred in hot water for making the wort.
A mixture of meal or bran and water fed to animals.
A mess; trouble.

Mash.etym: [Akin to G. meisch, maisch, meische, maische, mash, wash, and prob. to AS. miscian to mix. See Mix.]

senses.d: To convert into a mash; to reduce to a soft pulpy state by beating or pressure; to bruise; to crush; as, to mash apples in a mill, or potatoes with a pestle. Specifically (Brewing), to convert, as malt, or malt and meal, into the mash which makes wort.

Mash.etym: [Akin to G. meischen, maischen, to mash, mix, and prob. to mischen, E. mix. See 2d Mash.]

senses.d: One whose occupation is to build with stone or brick; also, one who prepares stone for building purposes.
A member of the fraternity of Freemasons. See Freemason.

Mason.etym: [F. maçon, LL. macio, machio, mattio, mactio, marcio, macerio; of uncertain origin.]

senses.d: To build stonework or brickwork about, under, in, over, etc.; to construct by masons; — with a prepositional suffix; as, to mason up a well or terrace; to mason in a kettle or boiler.
The fruit of the oak and beech, or other forest trees; nuts; acorns.
q: Oak mast, and beech, . . . they eat.
Swine under an oak filling themselves with the mast.

Mast.etym: [AS. mæst, fem.; akin to G. mast, and E. meat. See Meat.]

senses.d: A pole, or long, strong, round piece of timber, or spar, set upright in a boat or vessel, to sustain the sails, yards, rigging, etc. A mast may also consist of several pieces of timber united by iron bands, or of a hollow pillar of iron or steel.
q: The tallest pine Hewn on Norwegian hills, to be the mast Of some great ammiral.

senses.d: The vertical post of a derrick or crane.

Mast.etym: [AS. mæst, masc.; akin to D., G., Dan., & Sw. mast, Icel. mastr, and perh. to L. malus.]

senses.d: To furnish with a mast or masts; to put the masts of in position; as, to mast a ship.
A spar or strut to which tie wires or guys are attached for stiffening purposes.
A vessel having (so many) masts; — used only in compounds; as, a two-master.
A male person having another living being so far subject to his will, that he can, in the main, control his or its actions; — formerly used with much more extensive application than now.
One who uses, or controls at will, anything inanimate; as, to be master of one's time.
q: Master of a hundred thousand drachms.
We are masters of the sea.

senses.d: One who has attained great skill in the use or application of anything; as, a master of oratorical art.
q: Great masters of ridicule.
No care is taken to improve young men in their own language, that they may thoroughly understand and be masters of it.

senses.d: A title given by courtesy, now commonly pronounced mĭster, except when given to boys; — sometimes written Mister, but usually abbreviated to Mr.
A young gentleman; a lad, or small boy.
q: Where there are little masters and misses in a house, they are impediments to the diversions of the servants.

senses.d: The commander of a merchant vessel; — usually called captain. Also, a commissioned officer in the navy ranking next above ensign and below lieutenant; formerly, an officer on a man-of-war who had immediate charge, under the commander, of sailing the vessel.
A person holding an office of authority among the Freemasons, esp. the presiding officer; also, a person holding a similar office in other civic societies.
q: Throughout the city by the master gate.

Master.etym: [OE. maistre, maister, OF. maistre, mestre, F. maître, fr. L. magister, orig. a double comparative from the root of magnus great, akin to Gr. μέγασ. Cf. Maestro, Magister, Magistrate, Magnitude, Major, Mister, Mistress, Mickle.]

senses.d: To become the master of; to subject to one's will, control, or authority; to conquer; to overpower; to subdue.
q: Obstinacy and willful neglects must be mastered, even though it cost blows.

senses.d: To gain the command of, so as to understand or apply; to become an adept in; as, to master a science.
To own; to posses.
q: The wealth That the world masters.

senses.d: To be skillful; to excel.
The position or authority of a master; dominion; command; supremacy; superiority.
q: If divided by mountains, they will fight for the mastery of the passages of the tops.

senses.d: Superiority in war or competition; victory; triumph; preëminence.
q: The voice of them that shout for mastery.
Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things.
O, but to have gulled him Had been a mastery.

senses.d: Contest for superiority.
A masterly operation; a feat.
q: I will do a maistrie ere I go.

senses.d: Specifically, the philosopher's stone.
The act process of mastering; the state of having mastered.
q: He could attain to a mastery in all languages.
The learning and mastery of a tongue, being unpleasant in itself, should not be cumbered with other difficulties.

senses.d: A name given by coppersmiths to an alloy of copper, tin, iron, etc., usually called white metal.
Cast down; dejected; overthrown; slain.
q: When he saw them so piteous and so maat.

senses.d: A fabric of sedge, rushes, flags, husks, straw, hemp, or similar material, used for wiping and cleaning shoes at the door, for covering the floor of a hall or room, and for other purposes.
Any similar fabric for various uses, as for covering plant houses, putting beneath dishes or lamps on a table, securing rigging from friction, and the like.
Anything growing thickly, or closely interwoven, so as to resemble a mat in form or texture; as, a mat of weeds; a mat of hair.
An ornamental border made of paper, pasterboard, metal, etc., put under the glass which covers a framed picture; as, the mat of a daguerreotype.

Mat.etym: [AS. matt, meatt, fr. L. matta a mat made of rushes.]

senses.d: To cover or lay with mats.
To twist, twine, or felt together; to interweave into, or like, a mat; to entangle.
q: And o'er his eyebrows hung his matted hair.

senses.d: To grow thick together; to become interwoven or felted together like a mat.
The Paraguay tea, being the dried leaf of the Brazilian holly (Ilex Paraguensis). The infusion has a pleasant odor, with an agreeable bitter taste, and is much used for tea in South America.
Same as Checkmate.

Mate.etym: [F. mat, abbrev. fr. échec et mat. See Checkmate.]

senses.d: To confuse; to confound.
To checkmate.

Mate.etym: [F. mater to fatigue, enfeeble, humiliate, checkmate. See Mate checkmate.]

senses.d: One who customarily associates with another; a companion; an associate; any object which is associated or combined with a similar object.
Hence, specifically, a husband or wife; and among the lower animals, one of a pair associated for propagation and the care of their young.
A suitable companion; a match; an equal.
q: Ye knew me once no mate For you; there sitting where you durst not soar.

senses.d: An officer in a merchant vessel ranking next below the captain. If there are more than one bearing the title, they are called, respectively, first mate, second mate, third mate, etc. In the navy, a subordinate officer or assistant; as, master's mate; surgeon's mate.

Mate.etym: [Perhaps for older make a companion; cf. also OD. maet companion, mate, D. maat. Cf. Make a companion, Match a mate.]

senses.d: To match; to marry.
q: If she be mated with an equal husband.

senses.d: To match one's self against; to oppose as equal; to compete with.
q: There is no passion in the mind of man so weak but it mates and masters the fear of death.
I, . . . in the way of loyalty and truth, . . . Dare mate a sounder man than Surrey can be.

senses.d: To be or become a mate or mates, especially in sexual companionship; as, some birds mate for life; this bird will not mate with that one.
The womb.
q: All that openeth the matrix is mine.

senses.d: Hence, that which gives form or origin to anything
The lifeless portion of tissue, either animal or vegetable, situated between the cells; the intercellular substance.
A rectangular arrangement of symbols in rows and columns. The symbols may express quantities or operations.

Matrix.etym: [L., fr. mater mother. See Mother, and cf. Matrice.]

senses.d: A partly reduced copper sulphide, obtained by alternately roasting and melting copper ore in separating the metal from associated iron ores, and called coarse metal, fine metal, etc., according to the grade of fineness. On the exterior it is dark brown or black, but on a fresh surface is yellow or bronzy in color.
A dead or dull finish, as in gilding where the gold leaf is not burnished, or in painting where the surface is purposely deprived of gloss.

Matte.etym: [F. matte; cf. F. mat, masc., matte, fem., faint, dull, dim; — said of metals. See Mate checkmate.]

senses.d: That of which anything is composed; constituent substance; material; the material or substantial part of anything; the constituent elements of conception; that into which a notion may be analyzed; the essence; the pith; the embodiment.
q: He is the matter of virtue.

senses.d: That of which the sensible universe and all existent bodies are composed; anything which has extension, occupies space, or is perceptible by the senses; body; substance.

That with regard to, or about which, anything takes place or is done; the thing aimed at, treated of, or treated; subject of action, discussion, consideration, feeling, complaint, legal action, or the like; theme.
q: Son of God, Savior of men ! Thy name Shall be the copious matter of my song.
Every great matter they shall bring unto thee, but every small matter they shall judge.

senses.d: That which one has to treat, or with which one has to do; concern; affair; business.
q: To help the matter, the alchemists call in many vanities out of astrology.
Some young female seems to have carried matters so far, that she is ripe for asking advice.

senses.d: Affair worthy of account; thing of consequence; importance; significance; moment; — chiefly in the phrases what matter ? no matter, and the like.
q: A prophet some, and some a poet, cry; No matter which, so neither of them lie.

senses.d: Inducing cause or occasion, especially of anything disagreeable or distressing; difficulty; trouble.
q: And this is the matter why interpreters upon that passage in Hosea will not consent it to be a true story, that the prophet took a harlot to wife.

senses.d: Amount; quantity; portion; space; — often indefinite.
q: Away he goes, . . . a matter of seven miles.
I have thoughts to tarry a small matter.
No small matter of British forces were commanded over sea the year before.

senses.d: Substance excreted from living animal bodies; that which is thrown out or discharged in a tumor, boil, or abscess; pus; purulent substance.
That which is permanent, or is supposed to be given, and in or upon which changes are effected by psychological or physical processes and relations; — opposed to form.
Written manuscript, or anything to be set in type; copy; also, type set up and ready to be used, or which has been used, in printing.
q: Waller, with Sir William Balfour, exceeded in horse, but were, upon the whole matter, equal in foot.

Matter.etym: [OE. matere, F. matière, fr. L. materia; perh. akin to L. mater mother. Cf. Mother, Madeira, Material.]

senses.d: To be of importance; to import; to signify.
q: It matters not how they were called.

senses.d: To form pus or matter, as an abscess; to maturate.
To regard as important; to take account of; to care for.
q: He did not matter cold nor hunger.

senses.d: An implement for digging and grubbing. The head has two long steel blades, one like an adz and the other like a narrow ax or the point of a pickax.
q: 'T is you must dig with mattock and with spade.

senses.d: A heavy wooden hammer or beetle.
To beat and bruise with a heavy stick or cudgel; to wound in a coarse manner.
q: Meek modern faith to murder, hack, and maul.

senses.d: To injure greatly; to do much harm to.
q: It mauls not only the person misrepreseted, but him also to whom he is misrepresented.

senses.d: A gull.
A stomach; the receptacle into which food is taken by swallowing; in birds, the craw; — now used only of the lower animals, exept humorously or in contempt.
q: Bellies and maws of living creatures.

senses.d: Appetite; inclination.
q: Unless you had more maw to do me good.

Maw.etym: [OE. mawe, AS. maga stomach; akin to D. maag, OHG. mago, G. magen, Icel. magi, Sw. mage, Dan. mave. √103.]

senses.d: An old game at cards.
An auxiliary verb qualifying the meaning of another verb, by expressing:
Ability, competency, or possibility; — now oftener expressed by can.
q: How may a man, said he, with idle speech, Be won to spoil the castle of his health !
For what he may do is of two kinds; what he may do as just, and what he may do as possible.
For of all sad words of tongue or pen The saddest are these: “It might have been.”

senses.d: Liberty; permission; allowance.
q: Thou mayst be no longer steward.

senses.d: Contingency or liability; possibility or probability.
q: Though what he learns he speaks, and may advance Some general maxims, or be right by chance.

senses.d: Modesty, courtesy, or concession, or a desire to soften a question or remark.
q: How old may Phillis be, you ask.

senses.d: Desire or wish, as in prayer, imprecation, benediction, and the like.

May.etym: [AS. pres. mæg I am able, pret. meahte, mihte; akin to D. mogen, G. mögen, OHG. mugan, magan, Icel. mega, Goth. magan, Russ. moche. √103. Cf. Dismay, Main strength, Might. The old imp. mought is obsolete, except as a provincial word.]

senses.d: A maiden.

May.etym: [Cf. Icel. mær, Goth. mawi; akin to E. maiden. √103.]

senses.d: The fifth month of the year, containing thirty-one days.
The early part or springtime of life.
q: His May of youth, and bloom of lustihood.

senses.d: The flowers of the hawthorn; — so called from their time of blossoming; also, the hawthorn.
q: The palm and may make country houses gay.
Plumes that mocked the may.

senses.d: The merrymaking of May Day.

May.etym: [F. Mai, L. Maius; so named in honor of the goddess Maia (Gr. �), daughter of Atlas and mother of Mercury by Jupiter.]

senses.d: One. See Men, pron.

The person speaking, regarded as an object; myself; a pronoun of the first person used as the objective and dative case of the pronoum I; as, he struck me; he gave me the money, or he gave the money to me; he got me a hat, or he got a hat for me.
q: Me rather had my heart might frrl your love Than my unpleased eye see your courtesy.

Me.etym: [AS. mē, dat. & acc., mec, acc. only ; akin to D. mij, G. mich, Icel. & Goth. mik, L. me, Gr. μέ, εμἔ, Skr. mā, mām. √187. Cf. 2d Mine.]

senses.d: A tract of low or level land producing grass which is mown for hay; any field on which grass is grown for hay.
Low land covered with coarse grass or rank herbage near rives and in marshy places by the sea; as, the salt meadows near Newark Bay.

Meadow.etym: [AS. meady; akin to mǣd, and to G. matte; prob. also to E. mow. See Mow to cut (grass), and cf. 2d Mead.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a meadow; of the nature of a meadow; produced, growing, or living in, a meadow.
A part; a fragment; a portion.

Meal.etym: [OE. mele, AS. mǣl part, portion, portion of time; akin to E. meal a repast. Cf. Piecemeal.]

senses.d: The portion of food taken at a particular time for the satisfaction of appetite; the quantity usually taken at one time with the purpose of satisfying hunger; a repast; the act or time of eating a meal; as, the traveler has not eaten a good meal for a week; there was silence during the meal.
q: What strange fish Hath made his meal on thee ?

Meal.etym: [OE. mel; akin to E. meal a part, and to D. maal time, meal, G. mal time, mahl meal, Icel. māl measure, time, meal, Goth. mēl time, and to E. measure. See Measure.]

senses.d: Grain (esp. maize, rye, or oats) that is coarsely ground and unbolted; also, a kind of flour made from beans, pease, etc.; sometimes, any flour, esp. if coarse.
Any substance that is coarsely pulverized like meal, but not granulated.

Meal.etym: [OE. mele, AS. melu, melo; akin to D. meel, G. mehl, OHG. melo, Icel. mjöl, SW. mjöl, Dan. meel, also to D. malen to grind, G. mahlen, OHG., OS., & Goth. malan, Icel. mala, W. malu, L. molere, Gr. μύλη mill, and E. mill. √108. Cf. Mill, Mold soil, Mole an animal, Immolate, Molar.]

senses.d: To sprinkle with, or as with, meal.
To pulverize; as, mealed powder.
The usual time of eating a meal.
To have in the mind, as a purpose, intention, etc.; to intend; to purpose; to design; as, what do you mean to do ?
q: What mean ye by this service ?
Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.
I am not a Spaniard To say that it is yours and not to mean it.

senses.d: To signify; to indicate; to import; to denote.
q: What mean these seven ewe lambs ?
Go ye, and learn what that meaneth.

Mean.etym: [OE. menen, AS. mǣnan to recite, tell, intend, wish; akin to OS. mēnian to have in mind, mean, D. meenen, G. meinen, OHG. meinan, Icel. meina, Sw. mena, Dan. mene, and to E. mind. √104. See Mind, and cf. Moan.]

senses.d: To have a purpose or intention.
Destitute of distinction or eminence; common; low; vulgar; humble.
q: The mean man boweth down, and the great man humbleth himself.

senses.d: Wanting dignity of mind; low-minded; base; destitute of honor; spiritless; as, a mean motive.
q: Can you imagine I so mean could prove, To save my life by changing of my love ?

senses.d: Of little value or account; worthy of little or no regard; contemptible; despicable.
q: The Roman legions and great Cæsar found Our fathers no mean foes.

senses.d: Of poor quality; as, mean fare.
Penurious; stingy; close-fisted; illiberal; as, mean hospitality.

Mean.syn: Base; ignoble; abject; beggarly; wretched; degraded; degenerate; vulgar; vile; servile; menial; spiritless; groveling; slavish; dishonorable; disgraceful; shameful; despicable; contemptible; paltry; sordid. See Base.
Mean.etym: [OE. mene, AS. mǣne wicked; akin to mān, a., wicked, n., wickedness, OS. mēn wickedness, OHG. mein, G. meineid perjury, Icel. mein harm, hurt, and perh. to AS. gemǣne common, general, D. gemeen, G. gemein, Goth. gamáins, and L. communis. The AS. gemǣne prob. influenced the meaning.]

senses.d: Occupying a middle position; middle; being about midway between extremes.
q: Being of middle age and a mean stature.

senses.d: Intermediate in excellence of any kind.
q: According to the fittest style of lofty, mean, or lowly.

senses.d: Average; having an intermediate value between two extremes, or between the several successive values of a variable quantity during one cycle of variation; as, mean distance; mean motion; mean solar day.

Mean.etym: [OE. mene, OF. meiien, F. moyen, fr. L. medianus that is in the middle, fr. medius; akin to E. mid. See Mid.]

senses.d: That which is mean, or intermediate, between two extremes of place, time, or number; the middle point or place; middle rate or degree; mediocrity; medium; absence of extremes or excess; moderation; measure.
q: But to speak in a mean, the virtue of prosperity is temperance; the virtue of adversity is fortitude.
There is a mean in all things.
The extremes we have mentioned, between which the wellinstracted Christian holds the mean, are correlatives.

senses.d: A quantity having an intermediate value between several others, from which it is derived, and of which it expresses the resultant value; usually, unless otherwise specified, it is the simple average, formed by adding the quantities together and dividing by their number, which is called an arithmetical mean. A geometrical mean is the square root of the product of the quantities.
That through which, or by the help of which, an end is attained; something tending to an object desired; intermediate agency or measure; necessary condition or coagent; instrument.
q: Their virtuous conversation was a mean to work the conversion of the heathen to Christ.
You may be able, by this mean, to review your own scientific acquirements.
Philosophical doubt is not an end, but a mean.
By this means he had them more at vantage.
What other means is left unto us.

senses.d: Hence: Resources; property, revenue, or the like, considered as the condition of easy livelihood, or an instrumentality at command for effecting any purpose; disposable force or substance.
q: Your means are very slender, and your waste is great.

senses.d: A part, whether alto or tenor, intermediate between the soprano and base; a middle part.
q: The mean is drowned with your unruly base.

senses.d: Meantime; meanwhile.
A mediator; a go-between.
q: He wooeth her by means and by brokage.

senses.d: That which is meant or intended; intent; purpose; aim; object; as, a mischievous meaning was apparent.
q: If there be any good meaning towards you.

senses.d: That which is signified, whether by act lanquage; signification; sense; import; as, the meaning of a hint.
Sense; power of thinking.

A standard of dimension; a fixed unit of quantity or extent; an extent or quantity in the fractions or multiples of which anything is estimated and stated; hence, a rule by which anything is adjusted or judged.
An instrument by means of which size or quantity is measured, as a graduated line, rod, vessel, or the like.
q: False ells and measures be brought all clean adown.

senses.d: The dimensions or capacity of anything, reckoned according to some standard; size or extent, determined and stated; estimated extent; as, to take one's measure for a coat.
q: The measure thereof is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea.

senses.d: The contents of a vessel by which quantity is measured; a quantity determined by a standard; a stated or limited quantity or amount.
q: It is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of meal.

senses.d: Extent or degree not excessive or beyong bounds; moderation; due restraint; esp. in the phrases, in measure; with measure; without or beyond measure.
q: Hell hath enlarged herself, and opened her mouth without measure.

senses.d: Determined extent, not to be exceeded; limit; allotted share, as of action, influence, ability, or the like; due proportion.
q: Lord, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days.

senses.d: The quantity determined by measuring, especially in buying and selling; as, to give good or full measure.
Undefined quantity; extent; degree.
q: There is a great measure of discretion to be used in the performance of confession.

senses.d: Regulated division of movement
A number which is contained in a given number a number of times without a remainder; as in the phrases, the common measure, the greatest common measure, etc., of two or more numbers.
A step or definite part of a progressive course or policy; a means to an end; an act designed for the accomplishment of an object; as, political measures; prudent measures; an inefficient measure.
q: His majesty found what wrong measures he had taken in the conferring that trust, and lamented his error.

senses.d: The act of measuring; measurement.

Measure.etym: [OE. mesure, F. mesure, L. mensura, fr. metiri, mensus, to measure; akin to metrum poetical measure, Gr. μέτρον, E. meter. Cf. Immense, Mensuration, Mete to measure.]

senses.d: To ascertain by use of a measuring instrument; to compute or ascertain the extent, quantity, dimensions, or capacity of, by a certain rule or standard; to take the dimensions of; hence, to estimate; to judge of; to value; to appraise.
q: Great are thy works, Jehovah, infinite Thy power! what thought can measure thee?

senses.d: To serve as the measure of; as, the thermometer measures changes of temperature.
To pass throught or over in journeying, as if laying off and determining the distance.
q: A true devoted pilgrim is not weary To measure kingdoms with his feeble steps.

senses.d: To adjust by a rule or standard.
q: To secure a contented spirit, measure your desires by your fortunes, not your fortunes by your desires.

senses.d: To allot or distribute by measure; to set off or apart by measure; — often with out or off.
q: With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
That portion of eternity which is called time, measured out by the sun.

Measure.etym: [F. mesurer, L. mensurare. See Measure, n.]

senses.d: To make a measurement or measurements.
To result, or turn out, on measuring; as, the grain measures well; the pieces measure unequally.

To be of a certain size or quantity, or to have a certain length, breadth, or thickness, or a certain capacity according to a standard measure; as, cloth measures three fourths of a yard; a tree measures three feet in diameter.
Regulated or determined by a standard; hence, equal; uniform; graduated; limited; moderated; as, he walked with measured steps; he expressed himself in no measured terms.
Used in, or adapted for, ascertaining measurements, or dividing by measure.
Food, in general; anything eaten for nourishment, either by man or beast. Hence, the edible part of anything; as, the meat of a lobster, a nut, or an egg.
q: And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, . . . to you it shall be for meat.
Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you.

senses.d: The flesh of animals used as food; esp., animal muscle; as, a breakfast of bread and fruit without meat.
Specifically, dinner; the chief meal.

Meat.etym: [OE. mete, AS. mete; akin to OS. mat, meti, D. met hashed meat, G. mettwurst sausage, OHG. maz food, Icel. matr, Sw. mat, Dan. mad, Goth. mats. Cf. Mast fruit, Mush.]

senses.d: To supply with food.
q: His shield well lined, his horses meated well.

senses.d: To mix; to mingle.
q: More to know Did never meddle with my thoughts.

senses.d: To interest or engage one's self; to have to do; — in a good sense.
q: Study to be quiet, and to meddle with your own business.

senses.d: To interest or engage one's self unnecessarily or impertinently, to interfere or busy one's self improperly with another's affairs; specifically, to handle or distrub another's property without permission; — often followed by with or in.
q: Why shouldst thou meddle to thy hurt?
The civil lawyers . . . have meddled in a matter that belongs not to them.

Meddle.etym: [OE. medlen to mix, OF. medler, mesler, F. mêler, LL. misculare, a dim. fr. L. miscere to mix. √271. See Mix, and cf. Medley, Mellay.]

senses.d: To mix; to mingle.
q: “Wine meddled with gall.”

senses.d: Meddlesome.
A native or inhabitant of Media in Asia.

One of the sonant mutes β, δ, γ (b, d, g), in Greek, or of their equivalents in other languages, so named as intermediate between the tenues, π, τ, κ (p, t, k), and the aspiratæ (aspirates) φ, θ, χ (ph or f, th, ch). Also called middle mute, or medial, and sometimes soft mute.
Being in the middle; running through the middle; as, a median groove.
Situated in the middle; lying in a plane dividing a bilateral animal into right and left halves; — said of unpaired organs and parts; as, median coverts.

Median.etym: [L. medianus, fr. medius middle. See Medial.]

senses.d: A median line or point.
One who mediates; especially, one who interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them; hence, an intercessor.
q: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

senses.d: The science which relates to the prevention, cure, or alleviation of disease.
Any substance administered in the treatment of disease; a remedial agent; a remedy; physic.
q: By medicine, life may be prolonged.

senses.d: A philter or love potion.
A physician.

Medicine.etym: [L. medicina (sc. ars), fr. medicinus medical, fr. medicus: cf. F. médecine. See Medical.]

senses.d: To give medicine to; to affect as a medicine does; to remedy; to cure.

Among the North American Indians, any object supposed to give control over natural or magical forces, to act as a protective charm, or to cause healing; also, magical power itself; the potency which a charm, token, or rite is supposed to exert.
q: The North American Indian boy usually took as his medicine the first animal of which he dreamed during the long and solitary fast that he observed at puberty.

senses.d: Hence, a similar object or agency among other savages.
Short for Medicine man.
Intoxicating liquor; drink.
To keep the mind in a state of contemplation; to dwell on anything in thought; to think seriously; to muse; to cogitate; to reflect.
q: In his law doth he meditate day and night.

Meditate.etym: [L. meditatus, p. p. of meditari to meditate; cf. Gr. � to learn, E. mind.]

senses.d: To contemplate; to keep the mind fixed upon; to study.
To purpose; to intend; to design; to plan by revolving in the mind; as, to meditate a war.
q: I meditate to pass the remainder of life in a state of undisturbed repose.

Meditate.syn: To consider; ponder; weigh; revolve; study.

senses.d: The act of meditating; close or continued thought; the turning or revolving of a subject in the mind; serious contemplation; reflection; musing.
q: Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in thy sight.

senses.d: Thought; — without regard to kind.
q: With wings as swift As meditation or the thoughts of love.

Meditation.etym: [OE. meditacioun, F. méditation, fr. L. meditatio.]

senses.d: Mild of temper; not easily provoked or orritated; patient under injuries; not vain, or haughty, or resentful; forbearing; submissive.
q: Now the man Moses was very meek.

senses.d: Evincing mildness of temper, or patience; characterized by mildness or patience; as, a meek answer; a meek face.

Meek.syn: Gentle; mild; soft; yielding; pacific; unassuming; humble. See Gentle.
Meek.etym: [OE. mek, meoc; akin to Icel. mj�kr mild, soft, Sw. mjuk, Dan. myg, D. muik, Goth. mukamōdei gentleness.]

senses.d: To make meek; to nurture in gentleness and humility.
The quality or state of being meek.

To join, or come in contact with; esp., to come in contact with by approach from an opposite direction; to come upon or against, front to front, as distinguished from contact by following and overtaking.
To come in collision with; to confront in conflict; to encounter hostilely; as, they met the enemy and defeated them; the ship met opposing winds and currents.

To come into the presence of without contact; to come close to; to intercept; to come within the perception, influence, or recognition of; as, to meet a train at a junction; to meet carriages or persons in the street; to meet friends at a party; sweet sounds met the ear.
q: His daughter came out to meet him.

senses.d: To perceive; to come to a knowledge of; to have personal acquaintance with; to experience; to suffer; as, the eye met a horrid sight; he met his fate.
q: Of vice or virtue, whether blest or curst, Which meets contempt, or which compassion first.

senses.d: To come up to; to be even with; to equal; to match; to satisfy; to ansver; as, to meet one's expectations; the supply meets the demand.

Meet.etym: [OE. meten, AS. mētan, fr. mōt, gemōt, a meeting; akin to OS. mōtian to meet, Icel. mæta, Goth. gamōtjan. See Moot, v. t.]

senses.d: To come together by mutual approach; esp., to come in contact, or into proximity, by approach from opposite directions; to join; to come face to face; to come in close relationship; as, we met in the street; two lines meet so as to form an angle.
q: O, when meet now Such pairs in love and mutual honor joined !

senses.d: To come together with hostile purpose; to have an encounter or conflict.
q: Weapons more violent, when next we meet, May serve to better us and worse our foes.

senses.d: To assemble together; to congregate; as, Congress meets on the first Monday of December.
q: They . . . appointed a day to meet together.

senses.d: To come together by mutual concessions; hence, to agree; to harmonize; to unite.
An assembling together; esp., the assembling of huntsmen for the hunt; also, the persons who so assemble, and the place of meeting.
Suitable; fit; proper; appropriate; qualified; convenient.
q: It was meet that we should make merry.

Meet.etym: [OE. mete fitting, moderate, scanty, AS. mǣte moderate; akin to gemet fit, meet, metan to mete, and G. mässig moderate, gemäss fitting. See Mete.]

senses.d: Meetly.
A coming together; an assembling; as, the meeting of Congress.
A junction, crossing, or union; as, the meeting of the roads or of two rivers.
A congregation; a collection of people; a convention; as, a large meeting; an harmonious meeting.
An assembly for worship; as, to attend meeting on Sunday; — in England, applied distinctively and disparagingly to the worshiping assemblies of Dissenters.
