Meeting.syn: Conference; assembly; company; convention; congregation; junction; confluence; union.

senses.d: A sweet or agreeable succession of sounds.
q: Lulled with sound of sweetest melody.

senses.d: A rhythmical succession of single tones, ranging for the most part within a given key, and so related together as to form a musical whole, having the unity of what is technically called a musical thought, at once pleasing to the ear and characteristic in expression.
The air or tune of a musical piece.

Melody.etym: [OE. melodie, F. mélodie, L. melodia, fr. Gr. � a singing, choral song, fr. � musical, melodious; μέλοσ song, tune + � song. See Ode.]

senses.d: The juicy fruit of certain cucurbitaceous plants, as the muskmelon, watermelon, and citron melon; also, the plant that produces the fruit.
A large, ornamental, marine, univalve shell of the genus Melo.

Melon.etym: [F., fr. L. melo, for melopepo an apple-shaped melon, Gr. μηλοπέπων ; μη̑λον apple + πέπων a species of large melon; cf. L. malum apple. Cf. Marmalade.]

senses.d: To reduce from a solid to a liquid state, as by heat; to liquefy; as, to melt wax, tallow, or lead; to melt ice or snow.
Hence: To soften, as by a warming or kindly influence; to relax; to render gentle or susceptible to mild influences; sometimes, in a bad sense, to take away the firmness of; to weaken.
q: Thou would'st have . . . melted down thy youth.
For pity melts the mind to love.

Melt.syn: To liquefy; fuse; thaw; mollify; soften.
Melt.etym: [AS. meltan; akin to Gr. μέλδειν, E. malt, and prob. to E. smelt, v. √108. Cf. Smelt, v., Malt, Milt the spleen.]

senses.d: To be changed from a solid to a liquid state under the influence of heat; as, butter and wax melt at moderate temperatures.
To dissolve; as, sugar melts in the mouth.
Hence: To be softened; to become tender, mild, or gentle; also, to be weakened or subdued, as by fear.
q: My soul melteth for heaviness.
Melting with tenderness and kind compassion.

senses.d: To lose distinct form or outline; to blend.
q: The soft, green, rounded hills, with their flowing outlines, overlapping and melting into each other.

senses.d: To disappear by being dispersed or dissipated; as, the fog melts away.
Liquefaction; the act of causing (something) to melt, or the process of becoming melted.
Causing to melt; becoming melted; — used literally or figuratively; as, a melting heat; a melting appeal; a melting mood.
To remember; to cause to remember; to mention.
A part of an animal capable of performing a distinct office; an organ; a limb.
q: We have many members in one body, and all members have not the same office.

senses.d: Hence, a part of a whole; an independent constituent of a body

Member.etym: [OE. membre, F. membre, fr. L. membrum; cf. Goth. mimz flesh, Skr. mamsa.]

senses.d: Serving to preserve remembrance; commemorative; as, a memorial building.
q: There high in air, memorial of my name, Fix the smooth oar, and bid me live to fame.

senses.d: Contained in memory; as, a memorial possession.
Mnemonic; assisting the memory.
q: This succession of Aspirate, Soft, and Hard, may be expressed by the memorial word ASH.

Memorial.etym: [F. mémorial, L. memorialis, fr. memoria. See Memory.]

senses.d: Anything intended to preserve the memory of a person or event; something which serves to keep something else in remembrance; a monument.
q: Churches have names; some as memorials of peace, some of wisdom, some in memory of the Trinity itself.

senses.d: A memorandum; a record.
A written representation of facts, addressed to the government, or to some branch of it, or to a society, etc., — often accompanied with a petition.
Memory; remembrance.
q: Precious is the memorial of the just.

senses.d: A species of informal state paper, much used in negotiation.
The faculty of the mind by which it retains the knowledge of previous thoughts, impressions, or events.
q: Memory is the purveyor of reason.

senses.d: The reach and positiveness with which a person can remember; the strength and trustworthiness of one's power to reach and represent or to recall the past; as, his memory was never wrong.
The actual and distinct retention and recognition of past ideas in the mind; remembrance; as, in memory of youth; memories of foreign lands.
The time within which past events can be or are remembered; as, within the memory of man.
q: And what, before thy memory, was done From the begining.

senses.d: Something, or an aggregate of things, remembered; hence, character, conduct, etc., as preserved in remembrance, history, or tradition; posthumous fame; as, the war became only a memory.
q: The memory of the just is blessed.
That ever-living man of memory, Henry the Fifth.
The Nonconformists . . . have, as a body, always venerated her memory.

senses.d: A memorial.
q: These weeds are memories of those worser hours.

Memory.etym: [OE. memorie, OF. memoire, memorie, F. mémoire, L. memoria, fr. memor mindful; cf. mora delay. Cf. Demur, Martyr, Memoir, Remember.]

senses.d: A man; one; — used with a verb in the singular, and corresponding to the present indefinite one or they.
q: Men moot give silver to the poure friars.
A privy thief, men clepeth death.

Men.etym: [OE. me, men. “Not the plural of man, but a weakened form of the word man itself.” Skeat.]

senses.d: To repair, as anything that is torn, broken, defaced, decayed, or the like; to restore from partial decay, injury, or defacement; to patch up; to put in shape or order again; to re-create; as, to mend a garment or a machine.
To alter for the better; to set right; to reform; hence, to quicken; as, to mend one's manners or pace.
q: The best service they could do the state was to mend the lives of the persons who composed it.

senses.d: To help, to advance, to further; to add to.
q: Though in some lands the grass is but short, yet it mends garden herbs and fruit.
You mend the jewel by the wearing it.

Mend.syn: To improve; help; better; emend; amend; correct; rectify; reform.

senses.d: To grow better; to advance to a better state; to become improved.
Having the monthly flow or discharge; menstruating.
Of or pertaining to the monthly flow; catamenial.

Menstruous.etym: [L. menstruus, fr. mensis month. Cf. Menstruum.]

senses.d: A speaking or notice of anything, — usually in a brief or cursory manner. Used especially in the phrase to make mention of.
q: I will make mention of thy righteousness.
And sleep in dull, cold marble, where no mention Of me more must be heard of.

Mention.etym: [OE. mencioun, F. mention, L. mentio, from the root of meminisse to remember. See Mind.]

senses.d: To make mention of; to speak briefly of; to name.
q: I will mention the loving-kindnesses of the Lord.

senses.d: The objects of commerce; whatever is usually bought or sold in trade, or market, or by merchants; wares; goods; commodities.
The act or business of trading; trade; traffic.
To trade; to carry on commerce.
To make merchandise of; to buy and sell.
One who traffics on a large scale, especially with foreign countries; a trafficker; a trader.
q: Others, like merchants, venture trade abroad.

senses.d: A trading vessel; a merchantman.
One who keeps a store or shop for the sale of goods; a shopkeeper.

Merchant.etym: [OE. marchant, OF. marcheant, F. marchand, fr. LL. mercatans, -antis, p. pr. of mercatare to negotiate, L. mercari to traffic, fr. merx, mercis, wares. See Market, Merit, and cf. Commerce.]

senses.d: Of, pertaining to, or employed in, trade or merchandise; as, the merchant service.
To be a merchant; to trade.
Full of mercy; having or exercising mercy; disposed to pity and spare offenders; unwilling to punish.
q: The Lord, the Lord God, merciful and gracious.
Be merciful, great duke, to men of mold.

senses.d: Unwilling to give pain; compassionate.
q: A merciful man will be merciful to his beast.

Merciful.syn: Compassionate; tender; humane; gracious; kind; mild; clement; benignant.

senses.d: Forbearance to inflict harm under circumstances of provocation, when one has the power to inflict it; compassionate treatment of an offender or adversary; clemency.
q: Examples of justice must be made for terror to some; examples of mercy for comfort to others.

senses.d: Compassionate treatment of the unfortunate and helpless; sometimes, favor, beneficence.
Disposition to exercise compassion or favor; pity; compassion; willingness to spare or to help.
q: In whom mercy lacketh and is not founden.

senses.d: A blessing regarded as a manifestation of compassion or favor.
q: The Father of mercies and the God of all comfort.

Mercy.etym: [OE. merci, F. merci, L. merces, mercedis, hire, pay, reward, LL., equiv. to misericordia pity, mercy. L. merces is prob. akin to merere to deserve, acquire. See Merit, and cf. Amerce.]

senses.d: A pool or lake.
A boundary.
To divide, limit, or bound.
q: Which meared her rule with Africa.

senses.d: A mare.
Unmixed; pure; entire; absolute; unqualified.
q: Then entered they the mere, main sea.
The sorrows of this world would be mere and unmixed.

senses.d: Only this, and nothing else; such, and no more; simple; bare; as, a mere boy; a mere form.
q: From mere success nothing can be concluded in favor of any nation.

senses.d: In a merry manner; with mirth; with gayety and laughter; jovially. See Mirth, and Merry.
q: Merrily sing, and sport, and play.

senses.d: Laughingly gay; overflowing with good humor and good spirits; jovial; inclined to laughter or play ; sportive.
q: They drank, and were merry with him.
I am never merry when I hear sweet music.

senses.d: Cheerful; joyous; not sad; happy.
q: Is any merry? let him sing psalms.

senses.d: Causing laughter, mirth, gladness, or delight; as, a merry jest.

Merry.syn: Cheerful; blithe; lively; sprightly; vivacious; gleeful; joyous; mirthful; jocund; sportive; hilarious.
Merry.etym: [OE. merie, mirie, murie, merry, pleasant, AS. merge, myrige, pleasant; cf. murge, adv.; prob. akin to OHG. murg, short, Goth. gamaúrgjan to shorten; cf. L. murcus a coward, who cuts off his thumb to escape military service; the Anglo-Saxon and English meanings coming from the idea of making the tim

senses.d: A kind of wild red cherry.
Mass; church service.
A quantity of food set on a table at one time; provision of food for a person or party for one meal; as, a mess of pottage; also, the food given to a beast at one time.
q: At their savory dinner set Of herbs and other country messes.

senses.d: A number of persons who eat together, and for whom food is prepared in common; especially, persons in the military or naval service who eat at the same table; as, the wardroom mess.
A set of four; — from the old practice of dividing companies into sets of four at dinner.
The milk given by a cow at one milking.
A disagreeable mixture or confusion of things; hence, a situation resulting from blundering or from misunderstanding; as, he made a mess of it.

Mess.etym: [OE. mes, OF. mets, LL. missum, p. p. of mittere to put, place (e. g., on the table), L. mittere to send. See Mission, and cf. Mass religious service.]

senses.d: To take meals with a mess; to belong to a mess; to eat (with others); as, I mess with the wardroom officers.
To supply with a mess.
To make a mess of; to disorder or muddle; to muss; to jumble; to disturb.
q: It was n't right either to be messing another man's sleep.

senses.d: Any notice, word, or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.
q: Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee.

senses.d: Hence, specifically, an official communication, not made in person, but delivered by a messenger; as, the President's message.

Message.etym: [F., fr. LL. missaticum, fr. L. mittere, missum, to send. See Mission, and cf. Messenger.]

senses.d: To bear as a message.
A messenger.

Message.etym: [OE., fr. OF. message, fr. LL. missaticus. See 1st Message.]

senses.d: One who bears a message; the bearer of a verbal or written communication, notice, or invitation, from one person to another, or to a public body; specifically, an office servant who bears messages.
One who, or that which, foreshows, or foretells.
q: Yon gray lines That fret the clouds are messengers of day.

senses.d: A hawser passed round the capstan, and having its two ends lashed together to form an endless rope or chain; — formerly used for heaving in the cable.
A person appointed to perform certain ministerial duties under bankrupt and insolvent laws, such as to take charge of the estate of the bankrupt or insolvent.

Messenger.syn: Carrier; intelligencer; courier; harbinger; forerunner; precursor; herald.
Messenger.etym: [OE. messager, OF. messagier, F. messager. See Message.]

senses.d: The expected king and deliverer of the Hebrews; the Savior; Christ.
q: And told them the Messiah now was born.

Messiah.etym: [Heb. māshīakh anointed, fr. māshakh to anoint. Cf. Messias.]

senses.d: The Messiah.
q: I know that Messias cometh, which is called Christ.

senses.d: Meat.
To meet.
To dream; also impersonally; as, me mette, I dreamed.
To find the quantity, dimensions, or capacity of, by any rule or standard; to measure.

Mete.etym: [AS. metan; akin to D. meten, G. messen, OHG. mezzan, Icel. meta, Sw. mäta, Goth. mitan, L. modus measure, moderation, modius a corn measure, Gr. � to rule, � a corn measure, and ultimately from the same root as E. measure, L. metiri to measure; cf. Skr. mā to measure. √99. Cf. Measure, Meet, a., Mo

senses.d: To measure.
Measure; limit; boundary; — used chiefly in the plural, and in the phrase metes and bounds.
A yard, staff, or rod, used as a measure.

Meteyard.etym: [AS. metgeard. See Mete to measure, and Yard stick.]

senses.d: A syllable applied to the third tone of the scale of C, i.e., to E, in European solmization, but to the third tone of any scale in the American system.
Denoting the middle part; as, in mid ocean.
q: No more the mounting larks, while Daphne sings, Shall list'ning in mid air suspend their wings.

senses.d: Occupying a middle position; middle; as, the mid finger; the mid hour of night.

Made with a somewhat elevated position of some certain part of the tongue, in relation to the palate; midway between the high and the low; — said of certain vowel sounds; as, ā (āle), ĕ (ĕll), ō (ōld). See Guide to Pronunciation, §§ 10, 11.

Mid.etym: [AS. midd; akin to OS. middi, D. mid (in comp.), OHG. mitti, Icel. miðr, Goth. midjis, L. medius, Gr. μέσοσ, Skr. madhya. √271. Cf. Amid, Middle, Midst, Mean, Mediate, Meridian, Mizzen, Moiety.]

senses.d: Middle.
q: About the mid of night come to my tent.

senses.d: The middle part of the day; noon.

Midday.etym: [AS. middæg. See Mid, a., and Day.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to noon; meridional; as, the midday sun.

Equally distant from the extreme either of a number of things or of one thing; mean; medial; as, the middle house in a row; a middle rank or station in life; flowers of middle summer; men of middle age.
Intermediate; intervening.
q: Will, seeking good, finds many middle ends.

Middle.etym: [OE. middel, AS. middel; akin to D. middel, OHG. muttil, G. mittel. √271. See Mid, a.]

senses.d: The point or part equally distant from the extremities or exterior limits, as of a line, a surface, or a solid; an intervening point or part in space, time, or order of series; the midst; central portion
the waist.
q: In this, as in most questions of state, there is a middle.

senses.d: Being in the middle, or nearest the middle; midmost.
The middle of the night; twelve o'clock at night.
q: The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve.

senses.d: Being in, or characteristic of, the middle of the night; as, midnight studies; midnight gloom.
The interior or central part or place; the middle; — used chiefly in the objective case after in; as, in the midst of the forest.
q: And when the devil had thrown him in the midst, he came out of him.
There is nothing . . . in the midst which might not have been placed in the beginning.

senses.d: Hence, figuratively, the condition of being surrounded or beset; the press; the burden; as, in the midst of official duties; in the midst of secular affairs.

Midst.etym: [From middest, in the middest, for older in middes, where -s is adverbial (orig. forming a genitive), or still older a midde, a midden, on midden. See Mid, and cf. Amidst.]

senses.d: In the midst of; amidst.
In the middle.
A woman who assists other women in childbirth; a female practitioner of the obstetric art.

Midwife.etym: [OE. midwif, fr. AS. mid with (akin to Gr. �) + � woman, wife. Properly, the woman or wife who is attendant upon a woman in childbirth. See Meta-, and Wife.]

senses.d: To assist in childbirth.
To perform the office of midwife.
To midwife.
Force or power of any kind, whether of body or mind; energy or intensity of purpose, feeling, or action; means or resources to effect an object; strength; force; power; ability; capacity.
q: What so strong, But wanting rest, will also want of might?
Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might.

Might.etym: [AS. meaht, miht, from the root of magan to be able, E. may; akin to D. magt, OS. maht, G. macht, Icel. māttr, Goth. mahts. √103. See May, v.]

senses.d: In a mighty manner; with might; with great earnestness; vigorously; powerfully.
q: Whereunto I also labor, striving according to his working, which worketh in me mightily.

senses.d: To a great degree; very much.
q: Practical jokes amused us mightily.

senses.d: Possessing might; having great power or authority.
q: Wise in heart, and mighty in strength.

senses.d: Accomplished by might; hence, extraordinary; wonderful.
Denoting an extraordinary degree or quality in respect of size, character, importance, consequences, etc.
q: Mighty was their fuss about little matters.

Mighty.etym: [AS. meahtig, mihtig; akin to G. mächtig, Goth. mahteigs. See Might, n.]

senses.d: A warrior of great force and courage.
In a great degree; very.
q: We have a mighty pleasant garden.

senses.d: Giving milk; — now applied only to beasts.
Tender; pitiful; weeping.

Milch.etym: [OE. milche; akin to G. melk, Icel. milkr, mjōlkr, and to E. milk. See Milk.]

senses.d: A growth of minute powdery or webby fungi, whitish or of different colors, found on various diseased or decaying substances.

Mildew.etym: [AS. meledeáw; akin to OHG. militou, G. mehlthau, mehltau; prob. orig. meaning, honeydew; cf. Goth. milip honey. See Mellifluous, and Dew.]

senses.d: To taint with mildew.
q: He . . . mildews the white wheat.

senses.d: To become tainted with mildew.
A certain measure of distance, being equivalent in England and the United States to 320 poles or rods, or 5,280 feet.

Mile.etym: [AS. mīl, fr. L. millia, milia; pl. of mille a thousand, i.e., milia passuum a thousand paces. Cf. Mill the tenth of a cent, Million.]

senses.d: A white fluid secreted by the mammary glands of female mammals for the nourishment of their young, consisting of minute globules of fat suspended in a solution of casein, albumin, milk sugar, and inorganic salts.
A kind of juice or sap, usually white in color, found in certain plants; latex. See Latex.
An emulsion made by bruising seeds; as, the milk of almonds, produced by pounding almonds with sugar and water.
The ripe, undischarged spat of an oyster.

Milk.etym: [AS. meoluc, meoloc, meolc, milc; akin to OFries. meloc, D. melk, G. milch, OHG. miluh, Icel. mjōlk, Sw. mjölk, Dan. melk, Goth. miluks, G. melken to milk, OHG. melchan, Lith. milszti, L. mulgere, Gr. αμἔλγειν. √107. Cf. Milch, Emulsion, Milt soft roe of fishes.]

senses.d: To draw or press milk from the breasts or udder of, by the hand or mouth; to withdraw the milk of.
q: I have given suck, and know How tender 't is to love the babe that milks me.

senses.d: To draw from the breasts or udder; to extract, as milk; as, to milk wholesome milk from healthy cows.
To draw anything from, as if by milking; to compel to yield profit or advantage; to plunder.
q: They milk an unfortunate estate as regularly as a dairyman does his stock.

senses.d: To draw or to yield milk.
To draw or to yield milk.
To give off small gas bubbles during the final part of the charging operation; — said of a storage battery.
A money of account of the United States, having the value of the tenth of a cent, or the thousandth of a dollar.
A machine for grinding or comminuting any substance, as grain, by rubbing and crushing it between two hard, rough, or indented surfaces; as, a gristmill, a coffee mill; a bone mill.
A machine used for expelling the juice, sap, etc., from vegetable tissues by pressure, or by pressure in combination with a grinding, or cutting process; as, a cider mill; a cane mill.
A machine for grinding and polishing; as, a lapidary mill.
A common name for various machines which produce a manufactured product, or change the form of a raw material by the continuous repetition of some simple action; as, a sawmill; a stamping mill, etc.
A building or collection of buildings with machinery by which the processes of manufacturing are carried on; as, a cotton mill; a powder mill; a rolling mill.
A hardened steel roller having a design in relief, used for imprinting a reversed copy of the design in a softer metal, as copper.
An excavation in rock, transverse to the workings, from which material for filling is obtained.
A milling cutter. See Illust. under Milling.
A pugilistic encounter.

Mill.etym: [OE. mille, melle, mulle, milne, AS. myln, mylen; akin to D. molen, G. mühle, OHG. mulī, mulīn, Icel. mylna; all prob. from L. molina, fr. mola millstone; prop., that which grinds, akin to molere to grind, Goth. malan, G. mahlen, and to E. meal. √108. See Meal flour, and cf. Moline.]

senses.d: To reduce to fine particles, or to small pieces, in a mill; to grind; to comminute.
To shape, finish, or transform by passing through a machine; specifically, to shape or dress, as metal, by means of a rotary cutter.
To make a raised border around the edges of, or to cut fine grooves or indentations across the edges of, as of a coin, or a screw head; also, to stamp in a coining press; to coin.
To pass through a fulling mill; to full, as cloth.
To beat with the fists.
To roll into bars, as steel.
To swim under water; — said of air-breathing creatures.
To undergo hulling, as maize.
To move in a circle, as cattle upon a plain.
q: The deer and the pig and the nilghar were milling round and round in a circle of eight or ten miles radius.

senses.d: To swim suddenly in a new direction; — said of whales.
To take part in a mill; to box.
Short for Treadmill.
The raised or ridged edge or surface made in milling anything, as a coin or screw.
To fill (a winze or interior incline) with broken ore, to be drawn out at the bottom.
To cause to mill, or circle round, as cattle.
The name of several cereal and forage grasses which bear an abundance of small roundish grains. The common millets of Germany and Southern Europe are Panicum miliaceum, and Setaria Italica.

Millet.etym: [F., dim. of mil, L. milium; akin to Gr. μελίνη, AS. mil.]

senses.d: The number of ten hundred thousand, or a thousand thousand, — written 1,000,000. See the Note under Hundred.
A very great number; an indefinitely large number.
q: Millions of truths that a man is not concerned to know.

senses.d: The mass of common people; — with the article the.
q: For the play, I remember, pleased not the million.

Million.etym: [F., from LL. millio, fr. L. mille a thousand. See Mile.]

senses.d: One of two circular stones used for grinding grain or other substance.
q: No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge.

senses.d: To cut into very small pieces; to chop fine; to hash; as, to mince meat.
To suppress or weaken the force of; to extenuate; to palliate; to tell by degrees, instead of directly and frankly; to clip, as words or expressions; to utter half and keep back half of.
q: I know no ways to mince it in love, but directly to say — “I love you.”
Siren, now mince the sin, And mollify damnation with a phrase.
If, to mince his meaning, I had either omitted some part of what he said, or taken from the strength of his expression, I certainly had wronged him.

senses.d: To affect; to make a parade of.

Mince.etym: [AS. minsian to grow less, dwindle, fr. min small; akin to G. minder less, Goth. minniza less, mins less, adv., L. minor, adj. (cf. Minor); or more likely fr. F. mincer to mince, prob. from (assumed) LL. minutiare. √101. See Minish.]

senses.d: To walk with short steps; to walk in a prim, affected manner.
q: The daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, . . . mincing as they go.
I 'll . . . turn two mincing steps Into a manly stride.

senses.d: To act or talk with affected nicety; to affect delicacy in manner.
A short, precise step; an affected manner.
That minces; characterized by primness or affected nicety.

The intellectual or rational faculty in man; the understanding; the intellect; the power that conceives, judges, or reasons; also, the entire spiritual nature; the soul; — often in distinction from the body.
q: By the mind of man we understand that in him which thinks, remembers, reasons, wills.
What we mean by mind is simply that which perceives, thinks, feels, wills, and desires.
Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
The mind shall banquet, though the body pine.

senses.d: The state, at any given time, of the faculties of thinking, willing, choosing, and the like; psychical activity or state; as: (a) Opinion; judgment; belief.
q: A fool uttereth all his mind.
Being so hard to me that brought your mind, I fear she'll prove as hard to you in telling her mind.

senses.d: Choice; inclination; liking; intent; will.
q: If it be your minds, then let none go forth.

senses.d: Courage; spirit.
Memory; remembrance; recollection; as, to have or keep in mind, to call to mind, to put in mind, etc.

Mind.etym: [AS. mynd, gemynd; akin to OHG. minna memory, love, G. minne love, Dan. minde mind, memory, remembrance, consent, vote, Sw. minne memory, Icel. minni, Goth. gamunds, L. mens, mentis, mind, Gr. μένοσ, Skr. manas mind, man to think. √104, 278. Cf. Comment, Man, Mean, v., 3d Mental, Mignonette, Minion,

senses.d: To fix the mind or thoughts on; to regard with attention; to treat as of consequence; to consider; to heed; to mark; to note.
q: My lord, you nod: you do not mind the play.

senses.d: To occupy one's self with; to employ one's self about; to attend to; as, to mind one's business.
q: Bidding him be a good child, and mind his book.

senses.d: To obey; as, to mind parents; the dog minds his master.
To have in mind; to purpose.
q: I mind to tell him plainly what I think.

senses.d: To put in mind; to remind.
q: He minded them of the mutability of all earthly things.
I do thee wrong to mind thee of it.

Mind.syn: To notice; mark; regard; obey. See Attend.
Mind.etym: [AS. myndian, gemyndīan to remember. See Mind, n.]

senses.d: To give attention or heed; to obey; as, the dog minds well.
Disposed; inclined; having a mind.
q: Joseph . . . was minded to put her away privily.
If men were minded to live virtuously.

senses.d: Bearing in mind; regardful; attentive; heedful; observant.
q: What is man, that thou art mindful of him?
I promise you to be mindful of your admonitions.

senses.d: Regard; mindfulness.

Belonging to me; my. Used as a pronominal to me; my. Used as a pronominal adjective in the predicate; as, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” Rom. xii. 19. Also, in the old style, used attributively, instead of my, before a noun beginning with a vowel.
q: I kept myself from mine iniquity.
When a man deceives me once, says the Italian proverb, it is his fault; when twice, it is mine.
This title honors me and mine.
She shall have me and mine.

Mine.etym: [OE. min, fr. AS. mīn; akin to D. mijn, OS., OFries., & OHG. mīn, G. mein, Sw. & Dan. min, Icel. minn, Goth. meins my, mine, meina of me, and E. me. √187. See Me, and cf. My.]

senses.d: To dig a mine or pit in the earth; to get ore, metals, coal, or precious stones, out of the earth; to dig in the earth for minerals; to dig a passage or cavity under anything in order to overthrow it by explosives or otherwise.
To form subterraneous tunnel or hole; to form a burrow or lodge in the earth; as, the mining cony.

Mine.etym: [F. miner, L. minare to drive animals, in LL. also, to lead, conduct, dig a mine (cf. E. lode, and lead to conduct), akin to L. minari to threaten; cf. Sp. mina mine, conduit, subterraneous canal, a spring or source of water, It. mina. See Menace, and cf. Mien.]

senses.d: To dig away, or otherwise remove, the substratum or foundation of; to lay a mine under; to sap; to undermine; hence, to ruin or destroy by slow degrees or secret means.
q: They mined the walls.
Too lazy to cut down these immense trees, the spoilers . . . had mined them, and placed a quantity of gunpowder in the cavity.

senses.d: To dig into, for ore or metal.
q: Lead veins have been traced . . . but they have not been mined.

senses.d: To get, as metals, out of the earth by digging.
q: The principal ore mined there is the bituminous cinnabar.

senses.d: A subterranean cavity or passage
Any place where ore, metals, or precious stones are got by digging or washing the soil; as, a placer mine.
Fig.: A rich source of wealth or other good.

Mine.etym: [F., fr. LL. mina. See Mine, v. i.]

senses.d: To mix; intermix; to combine or join, as an individual or part, with other parts, but commonly so as to be distinguishable in the product; to confuse; to confound.
q: There was . . . fire mingled with the hail.

senses.d: To associate or unite in society or by ties of relationship; to cause or allow to intermarry; to intermarry.
q: The holy seed have mingled themselves with the people of those lands.

senses.d: To deprive of purity by mixture; to contaminate.
q: A mingled, imperfect virtue.

senses.d: To put together; to join.
To make or prepare by mixing the ingredients of.
q: proceeded to mingle another draught.

Mingle.etym: [From OE. mengen, AS. mengan; akin to D. & G. mengen, Icel. menga, also to E. among, and possibly to mix. Cf. Among, Mongrel.]

senses.d: To become mixed or blended.
A mixture.
To diminish; to lessen.
q: The living of poor men thereby minished.

Minish.etym: [OE. menusen, F. menuiser to make small, cut small, fr. (assumed) LL. minutiare, for minutare, fr. L. minutus small. See Minute, a., and cf. Diminish, Minge.]

senses.d: A servant; a subordinate; an officer or assistant of inferior rank; hence, an agent, an instrument.
q: Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua.
I chose Camillo for the minister, to poison My friend Polixenes.

senses.d: An officer of justice.
q: I cry out the on the ministres, quod he, That shoulde keep and rule this cité.

senses.d: One to whom the sovereign or executive head of a government intrusts the management of affairs of state, or some department of such affairs.
q: Ministers to kings, whose eyes, ears, and hands they are, must be answerable to God and man.

senses.d: A representative of a government, sent to the court, or seat of government, of a foreign nation to transact diplomatic business.
One who serves at the altar; one who performs sacerdotal duties; the pastor of a church duly authorized or licensed to preach the gospel and administer the sacraments.

Minister.syn: Delegate; official; ambassador; clergyman; parson; priest.
Minister.etym: [OE. ministre, F. ministre, fr. L. minister, orig. a double comparative from the root of minor less, and hence meaning, an inferior, a servant. See 1st Minor, and cf. Master, Minstrel.]

senses.d: To furnish or apply; to afford; to supply; to administer.
q: He that ministereth seed to the sower.
We minister to God reason to suspect us.

Minister.etym: [OE. ministren, OF. ministrer, fr. L. ministrare. See Minister, n.]

senses.d: To act as a servant, attendant, or agent; to attend and serve; to perform service in any office, sacred or secular.
q: The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister.

senses.d: To supply or to things needful; esp., to supply consolation or remedies.
q: Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased?

senses.d: The act of ministering; service; ministry.
The act of ministering; ministration; service.
Agency; instrumentality.
q: The ordinary ministry of second causes.
The wicked ministry of arms.

senses.d: The office, duties, or functions of a minister, servant, or agent; ecclesiastical, executive, or ambassadorial function or profession.
The body of ministers of state; also, the clergy, as a body.
Administration; rule; term in power; as, the ministry of Pitt.

Ministry.etym: [L. ministerium. See Minister, n., and cf. Mystery a trade.]

senses.d: A minnow.

In the Middle Ages, one of an order of men who subsisted by the arts of poetry and music, and sang verses to the accompaniment of a harp or other instrument; in modern times, a poet; a bard; a singer and harper; a musician.

Minstrel.etym: [OE. minstrel, menestral, OF. menestrel, fr. LL. ministerialis servant, workman (cf. ministrellus harpist), fr. L. ministerium service. See Ministry, and cf. Ministerial.]

senses.d: The name of several aromatic labiate plants, mostly of the genus Mentha, yielding odoriferous essential oils by distillation. See Mentha.

Mint.etym: [AS. minte, fr. L. mentha, Gr. μίνθα, μίνθη.]

senses.d: A place where money is coined by public authority.
Any place regarded as a source of unlimited supply; the supply itself.
q: A mint of phrases in his brain.

Mint.etym: [AS. mynet money, coin, fr. L. moneta the mint, coined money, fr. Moneta, a surname of Juno, in whose at Rome money was coined; akin to monere to warn, admonish, AS. manian, and to E. mind. See Mind, and cf. Money, Monition.]

senses.d: To make by stamping, as money; to coin; to make and stamp into money.
To invent; to forge; to fabricate; to fashion.
q: Titles . . . of such natures as may be easily minted.

senses.d: A Russian village community.
Same as Emir.
A wonder or wonderful thing.
q: That miracle and queen of genus.

senses.d: Specifically: An event or effect contrary to the established constitution and course of things, or a deviation from the known laws of nature; a supernatural event, or one transcending the ordinary laws by which the universe is governed.
q: They considered not the miracle of the loaves.

senses.d: A miracle play.
A story or legend abounding in miracles.
q: When said was all this miracle.

Miracle.etym: [F., fr. L. miraculum, fr. mirari to wonder. See Marvel, and cf. Mirror.]

senses.d: To make wonderful.
An ant.

Mire.etym: [AS. mīre, mȳre; akin to D. mier, Icel. maurr, Dan. myre, Sw. myra; cf. also Ir. moirbh, Gr. μύρμηξ.]

senses.d: Deep mud; wet, spongy earth.
q: He his rider from the lofty steed Would have cast down and trod in dirty mire.

Mire.etym: [OE. mire, myre; akin to Icel. mȳrr swamp, Sw. myra marshy ground, and perh. to E. moss.]

senses.d: To cause or permit to stick fast in mire; to plunge or fix in mud; as, to mire a horse or wagon.
To soil with mud or foul matter.
q: Smirched thus and mired with infamy.

senses.d: To stick in mire.
Merriment; gayety accompanied with laughter; jollity.
q: Then will I cause to cease . . . from the streets of Jerusalem, the voice of mirth.

senses.d: That which causes merriment.

Mirth.syn: Merriment; joyousness; gladness; fun; frolic; glee; hilarity; festivity; jollity. See Gladness.
Mirth.etym: [OE. mirthe, murthe, merthe, AS. myrð, myrgð, merhð, mirhð. See Merry.]

senses.d: Abounding with deep mud; full of mire; muddy; as, a miry road.
Wrong; amiss.
To carry, or go, wrong; to fail of reaching a destination, or fail of the intended effect; to be unsuccessful; to suffer defeat.
q: My ships have all miscarried.
The cardinal's letters to the pope miscarried.

senses.d: To bring forth young before the proper time.

Harm; damage; esp., disarrangement of order; trouble or vexation caused by human agency or by some living being, intentionally or not; often, calamity, mishap; trivial evil caused by thoughtlessness, or in sport.
q: Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs.
The practice whereof shall, I hope, secure me from many mischiefs.

senses.d: Cause of trouble or vexation; trouble.
q: The mischief was, these allies would never allow that the common enemy was subdued.

Mischief.syn: Damage; harm; hurt; injury; detriment; evil; ill.
Mischief.etym: [OE. meschef bad result, OF. meschief; pref. mes- (L. minus less) + chief end, head, F. chef chief. See Minus, and Chief.]

senses.d: To do harm to.
Causing mischief; harmful; hurtful; — now often applied where the evil is done carelessly or in sport; as, a mischievous child.
q: This false, wily, doubling disposition is intolerably mischievous to society.

Mischievous.syn: Harmful; hurtful; detrimental; noxious; pernicious; destructive.

senses.d: Very unhappy; wretched.
q: What hopes delude thee, miserable man?

senses.d: Causing unhappiness or misery.
q: What 's more miserable than discontent?

senses.d: Worthless; mean; despicable; as, a miserable fellow; a miserable dinner.
q: Miserable comforters are ye all.

senses.d: Avaricious; niggardly; miserly.

Miserable.etym: [F. misérable, L. miserabilis, fr. miserari to lament, pity, fr. miser wretched. See Miser.]

senses.d: A miserable person.
In a miserable; unhappily; calamitously; wretchedly; meanly.
q: They were miserably entertained.
The fifth was miserably stabbed to death.

senses.d: Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress; woe.
q: Destruction and misery are in their ways.

senses.d: Cause of misery; calamity; misfortune.
q: When we our betters see bearing our woes, We scarcely think our miseries our foes.

senses.d: Covetousness; niggardliness; avarice.

Misery.syn: Wretchedness; torture; agony; torment; anguish; distress; calamity; misfortune.
Misery.etym: [OE. miserie, L. miseria, fr. miser wretched: cf. F. misère, OF. also, miserie.]

senses.d: A title of courtesy prefixed to the name of a girl or a woman who has not been married. See Mistress, 5.
A young unmarried woman or a girl; as, she is a miss of sixteen.
q: Gay vanity, with smiles and kisses, Was busy 'mongst the maids and misses.

senses.d: A kept mistress. See Mistress, 4.
In the game of three-card loo, an extra hand, dealt on the table, which may be substituted for the hand dealt to a player.

To fail of hitting, reaching, getting, finding, seeing, hearing, etc.; as, to miss the mark one shoots at; to miss the train by being late; to miss opportunites of getting knowledge; to miss the point or meaning of something said.
q: When a man misses his great end, happiness, he will acknowledge he judged not right.

senses.d: To omit; to fail to have or to do; to get without; to dispense with; — now seldom applied to persons.
q: She would never miss, one day, A walk so fine, a sight so gay.
We cannot miss him; he does make our fire, Fetch in our wood.

senses.d: To discover the absence or omission of; to feel the want of; to mourn the loss of; to want.
q: Neither missed we anything . . . Nothing was missed of all that pertained unto him.
What by me thou hast lost, thou least shalt miss.

Miss.etym: [AS. missan; akin to D. & G. missen, OHG. missan, Icel. missa, Sw. mista, Dan. miste. √100. See Mis-, pref.]

senses.d: To fail to hit; to fly wide; to deviate from the true direction.
q: Men observe when things hit, and not when they miss.
Flying bullets now, To execute his rage, appear too slow; They miss, or sweep but common souls away.

senses.d: To fail to obtain, learn, or find; — with of.
q: Upon the least reflection, we can not miss of them.

senses.d: To go wrong; to err.
q: Amongst the angels, a whole legion Of wicked sprites did fall from happy bliss; What wonder then if one, of women all, did miss?

senses.d: To be absent, deficient, or wanting.
q: What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

senses.d: The act of missing; failure to hit, reach, find, obtain, etc.
Loss; want; felt absence.
q: There will be no great miss of those which are lost.

senses.d: Mistake; error; fault.
q: He did without any great miss in the hardest points of grammar.

senses.d: Harm from mistake.
Absent from the place where it was expected to be found; lost; wanting; not present when called or looked for.
q: Neither was there aught missing unto them.
For a time caught up to God, as once Moses was in the mount, and missing long.

senses.d: Visible watery vapor suspended in the atmosphere, at or near the surface of the earth; fog.
Coarse, watery vapor, floating or falling in visible particles, approaching the form of rain; as, Scotch mist.
Hence, anything which dims or darkens, and obscures or intercepts vision.
q: His passion cast a mist before his sense.

Mist.etym: [AS. mist; akin to D. & Sw. mist, Icel. mistr, G. mist dung, Goth. maíhstus, AS. mīgan to make water, Icel. mīga, Lith. migla mist, Russ. mgla, L. mingere, meiere, to make water, Gr. � to make water, � mist, Skr. mih to make water, n., a mist m☞gha cloud. √102. Cf. Misle, Mizzle, Mixen.]

senses.d: To cloud; to cover with mist; to dim.
To rain in very fine drops; as, it mists.
A woman having power, authority, or ownership; a woman who exercises authority, is chief, etc.; the female head of a family, a school, etc.
q: The late queen's gentlewoman! a knight's daughter! To be her mistress' mistress!

senses.d: A woman well skilled in anything, or having the mastery over it.
q: A letter desires all young wives to make themselves mistresses of Wingate's Arithmetic.

senses.d: A woman regarded with love and devotion; she who has command over one's heart; a beloved object; a sweetheart.
A woman filling the place, but without the rights, of a wife; a concubine; a loose woman with whom one consorts habitually.
A title of courtesy formerly prefixed to the name of a woman, married or unmarried, but now superseded by the contracted forms, Mrs., for a married, and Miss, for an unmarried, woman.
q: Now Mistress Gilpin (careful soul).

senses.d: A married woman; a wife.
q: Several of the neighboring mistresses had assembled to witness the event of this memorable evening.

senses.d: The old name of the jack at bowls.

Mistress.etym: [OE. maistress, OF. maistresse, F. maîtresse, LL. magistrissa, for L. magistra, fem. of magister. See Master, Mister, and cf. Miss a young woman.]

senses.d: To wait upon a mistress; to be courting.
To treat or use improperly; to use to a bad purpose; to misapply; as, to misuse one's talents.
q: The sweet poison of misused wine.

senses.d: To abuse; to treat ill.
q: O, she misused me past the endurance of a block.

Misuse.etym: [F. mésuser. See Mis-, prefix from French, and Use.]

senses.d: Wrong use; misapplication; erroneous or improper use.
q: Words little suspected for any such misuse.

senses.d: Violence, or its effects.
A minute arachnid, of the order Acarina, of which there are many species; as, the cheese mite, sugar mite, harvest mite, etc. See Acarina.
A small coin formerly circulated in England, rated at about a third of a farthing. The name is also applied to a small coin used in Palestine in the time of Christ.
q: Two mites, which make a farthing.

senses.d: A small weight; one twentieth of a grain.
Anything very small; a minute object; a very little quantity or particle.
q: For in effect they be not worth a myte.

Mite.etym: [AS. mīte mite (in sense 1); akin to LG. mite, D. mijt, G. miete, OHG. mīza; cf. Goth. maitan to cut.]

senses.d: To cause a promiscuous interpenetration of the parts of, as of two or more substances with each other, or of one substance with others; to unite or blend into one mass or compound, as by stirring together; to mingle; to blend; as, to mix flour and salt; to mix wines.
q: Fair persuasions mixed with sugared words.

senses.d: To unite with in company; to join; to associate.
q: Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people.

senses.d: To form by mingling; to produce by the stirring together of ingredients; to compound of different parts.
q: Hast thou no poison mixed?
I have chosen an argument mixed of religious and civil considerations.

Mix.etym: [AS. miscan; akin to OHG. misken, G. mischen, Russ. mieshate, W. mysgu, Gael. measg, L. miscere, mixtum, Gr. μίσγειν, μιγνύναι, Skr. miçra mixed. The English word has been influenced by L. miscere, mixtum (cf. Mixture), and even the AS. miscan may have been borrowed fr. L. miscere. Cf. Admix, Mash t

senses.d: To become united into a compound; to be blended promiscuously together.
To associate; to mingle.
q: He had mixed Again in fancied safety with his kind.

senses.d: Formed by mixing; united; mingled; blended. See Mix, v. t. & i.
The act of mixing, or the state of being mixed; as, made by a mixture of ingredients.
That which results from mixing different ingredients together; a compound; as, to drink a mixture of molasses and water; — also, a medley.
q: There is also a mixture of good and evil wisely distributed by God, to serve the ends of his providence.

senses.d: An ingredient entering into a mixed mass; an additional ingredient.
q: Cicero doubts whether it were possible for a community to exist that had not a prevailing mixture of piety in its constitution.

senses.d: A kind of liquid medicine made up of many ingredients; esp., as opposed to solution, a liquid preparation in which the solid ingredients are not completely dissolved.

A mass of two or more ingredients, the particles of which are separable, independent, and uncompounded with each other, no matter how thoroughly and finely commingled; — contrasted with a compound; thus, gunpowder is a mechanical mixture of carbon, sulphur, and niter.

An organ stop, comprising from two to five ranges of pipes, used only in combination with the foundation and compound stops; — called also furniture stop. It consists of high harmonics, or overtones, of the ground tone.

Mixture.etym: [L. mixtura, fr. miscere, mixtum, to mix: cf. F. mixture. See Mix.]

senses.d: More; — usually, more in number.
q: An hundred thousand mo.
Likely to find mo to commend than to imitate it.

senses.d: One of the posterity of Moab, the son of Lot. (Gen. xix. 37.) Also used adjectively.
A female Moabite.
Moabite.
To imitate; to mimic; esp., to mimic in sport, contempt, or derision; to deride by mimicry.
q: To see the life as lively mocked as ever Still sleep mocked death.
Mocking marriage with a dame of France.

senses.d: To treat with scorn or contempt; to deride.
q: Elijah mocked them, and said, Cry aloud.
Let not ambition mock their useful toil.

senses.d: To disappoint the hopes of; to deceive; to tantalize; as, to mock expectation.
q: Thou hast mocked me, and told me lies.
He will not . . . Mock us with his blest sight, then snatch him hence.

Mock.syn: To deride; ridicule; taunt; jeer; tantalize; disappoint. See Deride.
Mock.etym: [F. moquer, of uncertain origin; cf. OD. mocken to mumble, G. mucken, OSw. mucka.]

senses.d: To make sport in contempt or in jest; to speak in a scornful or jeering manner.
q: When thou mockest, shall no man make thee ashamed?
She had mocked at his proposal.

senses.d: An act of ridicule or derision; a scornful or contemptuous act or speech; a sneer; a jibe; a jeer.
q: Fools make a mock at sin.

senses.d: Imitation; mimicry.
Imitating reality, but not real; false; counterfeit; assumed; sham.
q: That superior greatness and mock majesty.

senses.d: One who, or that which, mocks; a scorner; a scoffer; a derider.
A deceiver; an impostor.
A mocking bird.
Imitating, esp. in derision, or so as to cause derision; mimicking; derisive.
Manner of doing or being; method; form; fashion; custom; way; style; as, the mode of speaking; the mode of dressing.
q: The duty of itself being resolved on, the mode of doing it may easily be found.
A table richly spread in regal mode.

senses.d: Prevailing popular custom; fashion, especially in the phrase the mode.
q: The easy, apathetic graces of a man of the mode.

senses.d: Variety; gradation; degree.

Any combination of qualities or relations, considered apart from the substance to which they belong, and treated as entities; more generally, condition, or state of being; manner or form of arrangement or manifestation; form, as opposed to matter.
q: Modes I call such complex ideas, which, however compounded, contain not in them the supposition of subsisting by themselves, but are considered as dependencies on, or affections of, substances.

senses.d: The form in which the proposition connects the predicate and subject, whether by simple, contingent, or necessary assertion; the form of the syllogism, as determined by the quantity and quality of the constituent proposition; mood.
Same as Mood.
The scale as affected by the various positions in it of the minor intervals; as, the Dorian mode, the Ionic mode, etc., of ancient Greek music.
A kind of silk. See Alamode, n.

Mode.etym: [L. modus a measure, due or proper measure, bound, manner, form; akin to E. mete: cf. F. mode. See Mete, and cf. Commodious, Mood in grammar, Modus.]

senses.d: Kept within due bounds; observing reasonable limits; not excessive, extreme, violent, or rigorous; limited; restrained
Limited in quantity; sparing; temperate; frugal; as, moderate in eating or drinking; a moderate table.
Limited in degree of activity, energy, or excitement; reasonable; calm; slow; as, moderate language; moderate endeavors.
Not extreme in opinion, in partisanship, and the like; as, a moderate Calvinist.
q: A number of moderate members managed . . . to obtain a majority in a thin house.

senses.d: Not violent or rigorous; temperate; mild; gentle; as, a moderate winter.
Limited as to degree of progress; as, to travel at moderate speed.
Limited as to the degree in which a quality, principle, or faculty appears; as, an infusion of moderate strength; a man of moderate abilities.
Limited in scope or effects; as, a reformation of a moderate kind.

Moderate.etym: [L. moderatus, p. p. of moderate, moderati, to moderate, regulate, control, fr. modus measure. See Mode.]

senses.d: One of a party in the Church of Scotland in the 18th century, and part of the 19th, professing moderation in matters of church government, in discipline, and in doctrine.

To restrain from excess of any kind; to reduce from a state of violence, intensity, or excess; to keep within bounds; to make temperate; to lessen; to allay; to repress; to temper; to qualify; as, to moderate rage, action, desires, etc.; to moderate heat or wind.
q: By its astringent quality, it moderates the relaxing quality of warm water.
To moderate stiff minds disposed to strive.

senses.d: To preside over, direct, or regulate, as a public meeting; as, to moderate a synod.
To become less violent, severe, rigorous, or intense; as, the wind has moderated.
To preside as a moderator.
q: Dr. Barlow engaged . . . to moderate for him in the divinity disputation.

senses.d: In a moderate manner or degree; to a moderate extent.
q: Each nymph but moderately fair.

senses.d: The act of moderating, or of imposing due restraint.
The state or quality of being mmoderate.
q: In moderation placing all my glory, While Tories call me Whig, and Whigs a Tory.

senses.d: Calmness of mind; equanimity; as, to bear adversity with moderation.
q: The calm and judicious moderation of Orange.

senses.d: The first public examinations for degrees at the University of Oxford; — usually contracted to mods.
Restraining within due limits of propriety; not forward, bold, boastful, or presumptious; rather retiring than pushing one's self forward; not obstructive; as, a modest youth; a modest man.
Observing the proprieties of the sex; not unwomanly in act or bearing; free from undue familiarity, indecency, or lewdness; decent in speech and demeanor; — said of a woman.
q: Mrs. Ford, the honest woman, the modest wife.
The blushing beauties of a modest maid.

senses.d: Evincing modestly in the actor, author, or speaker; not showing presumption; not excessive or extreme; moderate; as, a modest request; modest joy.

Modest.syn: Reserved; unobtrusive; diffident; bashful; coy; shy; decent; becoming; chaste; virtuous.
Modest.etym: [F. modeste, L. modestus, fr. modus measure. See Mode.]

senses.d: Moderately wet; damp; humid; not dry; as, a moist atmosphere or air.
Fresh, or new.

Moist.etym: [OE. moiste, OF. moiste, F. moite, fr. L. muccidus, for mucidus, moldy, musty. Cf. Mucus, Mucid.]

senses.d: To moisten.
To make damp; to wet in a small degree.
q: A pipe a little moistened on the inside.

senses.d: To soften by making moist; to make tender.
q: It moistened not his executioner's heart with any pity.

senses.d: A moderate degree of wetness.
That which moistens or makes damp or wet; exuding fluid; liquid in small quantity.
q: All my body's moisture Scarce serves to quench my furnace-burning heat.

senses.d: A spot; a stain; a mark which discolors or disfigures.
A spot, mark, or small permanent protuberance on the human body; esp., a spot which is dark-colored, from which commonly issue one or more hairs.

Mole.etym: [AS. māl; akin to OHG. meil, Goth. mail Cf. Mail a spot.]

senses.d: A mass of fleshy or other more or less solid matter generated in the uterus.

A mound or massive work formed of masonry or large stones, etc., laid in the sea, often extended either in a right line or an arc of a circle before a port which it serves to defend from the violence of the waves, thus protecting ships in a harbor; also, sometimes, the harbor itself.

Mole.etym: [F. môle, L. moles. Cf. Demolish, Emolument, Molest.]

senses.d: Any insectivore of the family Talpidæ. They have minute eyes and ears, soft fur, and very large and strong fore feet.
A plow of peculiar construction, for forming underground drains.

Mole.etym: [OE. molle, either shortened fr. moldwerp, or from the root of E. mold soil: cf. D. mol, OD. molworp. See Moldwarp.]

senses.d: To form holes in, as a mole; to burrow; to excavate; as, to mole the earth.
To clear of molehills.
The fire god of the Ammonites, to whom human sacrifices were offered; Moloch.
To soften; to make tender; to reduce the hardness, harshness, or asperity of; to qualify; as, to mollify the ground.
q: With sweet science mollified their stubborn hearts.

senses.d: To assuage, as pain or irritation, to appease, as excited feeling or passion; to pacify; to calm.

Mollify.etym: [F. mollifier, L. mollificare; mollis soft + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Enmollient, Moil, v. t., and -fy.]

senses.d: The fire god of the Ammonites in Canaan, to whom human sacrifices were offered; Molech. Also applied figuratively.
A spiny Australian lizard (Moloch horridus). The horns on the head and numerous spines on the body give it a most formidable appearance.
Melted; being in a state of fusion, esp. when the liquid state is produced by a high degree of heat; as, molten iron.
Made by melting and casting the substance or metal of which the thing is formed; as, a molten image.
A minute portion of time; a point of time; an instant; as, at that very moment.
q: In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.

senses.d: Impulsive power; force; momentum.
q: The moments or quantities of motion in bodies.
Touch, with lightest moment of impulse, His free will.

senses.d: Importance, as in influence or effect; consequence; weight or value; consideration.
q: Matters of great moment.
It is an abstruse speculation, but also of far less moment and consequence of us than the others.

senses.d: An essential element; a deciding point, fact, or consideration; an essential or influential circumstance.
An infinitesimal change in a varying quantity; an increment or decrement.
Tendency, or measure of tendency, to produce motion, esp. motion about a fixed point or axis.

Moment.syn: Instant; twinkling; consequence; weight; force; value; consideration; signification; avail.
Moment.etym: [F. moment, L. momentum, for movimentum movement, motion, moment, fr. movere to move. See Move, and cf. Momentum, Movement.]

senses.d: A piece of metal, as gold, silver, copper, etc., coined, or stamped, and issued by the sovereign authority as a medium of exchange in financial transactions between citizens and with government; also, any number of such pieces; coin.
q: To prevent such abuses, . . . it has been found necessary . . . to affix a public stamp upon certain quantities of such particular metals, as were in those countries commonly made use of to purchase goods. Hence the origin of coined money, and of those public offices called mints.

senses.d: Any written or stamped promise, certificate, or order, as a government note, a bank note, a certificate of deposit, etc., which is payable in standard coined money and is lawfully current in lieu of it; in a comprehensive sense, any currency usually and lawfully employed in buying and selling.
In general, wealth; property; as, he has much money in land, or in stocks; to make, or lose, money.
q: The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.

Money.etym: [OE. moneie, OF. moneie, F. monnaie, fr. L. moneta. See Mint place where coin is made, Mind, and cf. Moidore, Monetary.]

senses.d: To supply with money.
Something of unnatural size, shape, or quality; a prodigy; an enormity; a marvel.
q: A monster or marvel.

senses.d: Specifically , an animal or plant departing greatly from the usual type, as by having too many limbs.
Any thing or person of unnatural or excessive ugliness, deformity, wickedness, or cruelty.

Monster.etym: [OE. monstre, F. monstre, fr. L. monstrum, orig., a divine omen, indicating misfortune; akin of monstrare to show, point out, indicate, and monere to warn. See Monition, and cf. Demonstrate, Muster.]

senses.d: Monstrous in size.
To make monstrous.

One of the twelve portions into which the year is divided; the twelfth part of a year, corresponding nearly to the length of a synodic revolution of the moon, — whence the name. In popular use, a period of four weeks is often called a month.

Month.etym: [OE. month, moneth, AS. mōnð, mōnað; akin to mōna moon, and to D. maand month, G. monat, OHG. mānōd, Icel. mānuðr, mānaðr, Goth. mēnōþs. √272. See Moon.]

senses.d: Continued a month, or a performed in a month; as, the monthly revolution of the moon.
Done, happening, payable, published, etc., once a month, or every month; as, a monthly visit; monthly charges; a monthly installment; a monthly magazine.
A publication which appears regularly once a month.
Once a month; in every month; as, the moon changes monthly.
As if under the influence of the moon; in the manner of a lunatic.
Something which stands, or remains, to keep in remembrance what is past; a memorial.
q: Of ancient British art A pleasing monument.
Our bruised arms hung up for monuments.

senses.d: A building, pillar, stone, or the like, erected to preserve the remembrance of a person, event, action, etc.; as, the Washington monument; the Bunker Hill monument. Also, a tomb, with memorial inscriptions.
q: On your family's old monument Hang mournful epitaphs, and do all rites That appertain unto a burial.

senses.d: A stone or other permanent object, serving to indicate a limit or to mark a boundary.
A saying, deed, or example, worthy of record.
q: Acts and Monuments of these latter and perilous days.

Monument.etym: [F., fr. L. monumentum, fr. monere to remind, admonish. See Monition, and cf. Moniment.]

senses.d: The celestial orb which revolves round the earth; the satellite of the earth; a secondary planet, whose light, borrowed from the sun, is reflected to the earth, and serves to dispel the darkness of night. The diameter of the moon is 2,160 miles, its mean distance from the earth is 240,000 miles, and its mass is one eightieth that of the earth. See Lunar month, under Month.
q: The crescent moon, the diadem of night.

senses.d: A secondary planet, or satellite, revolving about any member of the solar system; as, the moons of Jupiter or Saturn.
The time occupied by the moon in making one revolution in her orbit; a month.
A crescentlike outwork. See Half-moon.

Moon.etym: [OE. mone, AS. mōna; akin to D. maan, OS. & OHG. māno, G. mond, Icel. māni, Dan. maane, Sw. måne, Goth. mēna, Lith. menů, L. mensis month, Gr. μήνη moon, μήν month, Skr. mās moon, month; prob. from a root meaning to measure (cf. Skr. mā to measure), from its serving to measure the time. √271. Cf. Me

senses.d: To expose to the rays of the moon.
q: If they have it to be exceeding white indeed, they seethe it yet once more, after it hath been thus sunned and mooned.

senses.d: To act if moonstruck; to wander or gaze about in an abstracted manner.
q: Elsley was mooning down the river by himself.

senses.d: A hill.
A root.

More.etym: [AS. more, moru; akin to G. möhre carrot, OHG. moraha, morha.]

senses.d: Greater; superior; increased
q: He gat more money.
If we procure not to ourselves more woe.
Whilst sisters nine, which dwell on Parnasse height, Do make them music for their more delight.
The more part knew not wherefore they were come together.
Wrong not that wrong with a more contempt.

senses.d: Greater in number; exceeding in numbers; — with the plural.
q: The people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we.

senses.d: Additional; other; as, he wept because there were no more worlds to conquer.
q: With open arms received one poet more.

More.etym: [OE. more, mare, and (orig. neut. and adv.) mo, ma, AS. māra, and (as neut. and adv.) mā; akin to D. meer, OS. mēr, G. mehr, OHG. mēro, mēr, Icel. meiri, meirr, Dan. meere, meer, Sw. mera, mer, Goth. maiza, a., mais, adv., and perh. to L. major greater, compar. of magnus great, and magis, adv., more

senses.d: A greater quantity, amount, or number; that which exceeds or surpasses in any way what it is compared with.
q: And the children of Israel did so, and gathered, some more, some less.

senses.d: That which is in addition; something other and further; an additional or greater amount.
q: They that would have more and more can never have enough.
O! That pang where more than madness lies.

senses.d: In a greater quantity; in or to a greater extent or degree.
q: Admiring more The riches of Heaven's pavement.

senses.d: With an adjective or adverb (instead of the suffix -er) to form the comparative degree; as, more durable; more active; more sweetly.
q: Happy here, and more happy hereafter.

senses.d: In addition; further; besides; again.
q: Yet once more, O ye laurels, and once more, Ye myrtles brown, with ivy never sere, I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude.

senses.d: To make more; to increase.
Beyond what has been said; further; besides; in addition; furthermore; also; likewise.
q: Moreover, he hath left you all his walks.

senses.d: The first part of the day; the morning; — used chiefly in poetry.
q: From morn To noon he fell, from noon to dewy eve.

Morn.etym: [OE. morwen, morgen, AS. morgen; akin to D. morgen, OS. morgan, G. morgen, Icel. morginn, morgunn, Sw. morgon, Dan. morgen, Goth. maúrgins. Cf. Morrow, Morning.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the morn; morning.
A ring fitted upon the head of a lance to prevent wounding an adversary in tilting.

Morne.etym: [F., fr. morne sad, sorrowful. See Mourn.]

senses.d: The first or early part of the day, variously understood as the earliest hours of light, the time near sunrise; the time from midnight to noon, from rising to noon, etc.
The first or early part; as, the morning of life.
The goddess Aurora.
Pertaining to the first part or early part of the day; being in the early part of the day; as, morning dew; morning light; morning service.
q: She looks as clear As morning roses newly washed with dew.

senses.d: Morning.
q: We loved he by the morwe a sop in wine.

senses.d: The next following day; the day subsequent to any day specified or understood.
q: Till this stormy night is gone, And the eternal morrow dawn.

senses.d: The day following the present; to-morrow.

Morrow.etym: [OE. morwe, morwen, AS. morgen. See Morn.]

senses.d: A little bite or bit of food.
q: Every morsel to a satisfied hunger is only a new labor to a tired digestion.

senses.d: A small quantity; a little piece; a fragment.

Morsel.etym: [OF. morsel, F. morceau, LL. morsellus, a dim. fr. L. morsus a biting, bite, fr. mordere to bite; prob. akin to E. smart. See Smart, and cf. Morceau, Mordant, Muse, v., Muzzle, n.]

senses.d: A great quantity or number.
q: There was a mort of merrymaking.

Mort.etym: [Cf. Icel. margt, neut. of margr many.]

senses.d: A woman; a female.
q: Male gypsies all, not a mort among them.

senses.d: A salmon in its third year.
Death; esp., the death of game in the chase.
A note or series of notes sounded on a horn at the death of game.
q: The sportsman then sounded a treble mort.

senses.d: The skin of a sheep or lamb that has died of disease.
A variety of dummy whist for three players; also, the exposed or dummy hand in this game.
Subject to death; destined to die; as, man is mortal.
Destructive to life; causing or occasioning death; terminating life; exposing to or deserving death; deadly; as, a mortal wound; a mortal sin.
Fatally vulnerable; vital.
q: Last of all, against himself he turns his sword, but missing the mortal place, with his poniard finishes the work.

senses.d: Of or pertaining to the time of death.
q: Safe in the hand of one disposing Power, Or in the natal or the mortal hour.

senses.d: Affecting as if with power to kill; deathly.
q: The nymph grew pale, and in a mortal fright.

senses.d: Human; belonging to man, who is mortal; as, mortal wit or knowledge; mortal power.
q: The voice of God To mortal ear is dreadful.

senses.d: Very painful or tedious; wearisome; as, a sermon lasting two mortal hours.

Mortal.etym: [F. mortel, L. mortalis, from mors, mortis, death, fr. moriri 8die; akin to E. murder. See Murder, and cf. Filemot, Mere a lake, Mortgage.]

senses.d: A being subject to death; a human being; man.
The condition or quality of being mortal; subjection to death or to the necessity of dying.
q: When I saw her die, I then did think on your mortality.

senses.d: Human life; the life of a mortal being.
q: From this instant There 's nothing serious in mortality.

senses.d: Those who are, or that which is, mortal; the human race; humanity; human nature.
q: Take these tears, mortality's relief.

senses.d: Death; destruction.

The whole sum or number of deaths in a given time or a given community; also, the proportion of deaths to population, or to a specific number of the population; death rate; as, a time of great, or low, mortality; the mortality among the settlers was alarming.
In a mortal manner; so as to cause death; as, mortally wounded.
In the manner of a mortal or of mortal beings.
q: I was mortally brought forth.

senses.d: In an extreme degree; to the point of dying or causing death; desperately; as, mortally jealous.
q: Adrian mortally envied poets, painters, and artificers, in works wherein he had a vein to excel.

senses.d: A strong vessel, commonly in form of an inverted bell, in which substances are pounded or rubbed with a pestle.

A short piece of ordnance, used for throwing bombs, carcasses, shells, etc., at high angles of elevation, as 45°, and even higher; — so named from its resemblance in shape to the utensil above described.

Mortar.etym: [OE. morter, AS. mortēre, L. mortarium: cf. F. mortier mortar. Cf. sense 2 (below), also 2d Mortar, Martel, Morter.]

senses.d: A building material made by mixing lime, cement, or plaster of Paris, with sand, water, and sometimes other materials; — used in masonry for joining stones, bricks, etc., also for plastering, and in other ways.

Mortar.etym: [OE. mortier, F. mortier, L. mortarium mortar, a large basin or trough in which mortar is made, a mortar (in sense 1, above). See 1st Mortar.]

senses.d: To plaster or make fast with mortar.
A chamber lamp or light.

A conveyance of property, upon condition, as security for the payment of a debt or the preformance of a duty, and to become void upon payment or performance according to the stipulated terms; also, the written instrument by which the conveyance is made.
State of being pledged; as, lands given in mortgage.

Mortgage.etym: [F. mort-gage; mort dead (L. mortuus) + gage pledge. See Mortal, and Gage.]

senses.d: To grant or convey, as property, for the security of a debt, or other engagement, upon a condition that if the debt or engagement shall be discharged according to the contract, the conveyance shall be void, otherwise to become absolute, subject, however, to the right of redemption.
Hence: To pledge, either literally or figuratively; to make subject to a claim or obligation.
q: Mortgaging their lives to covetise.
I myself an mortgaged to thy will.

senses.d: To destroy the organic texture and vital functions of; to produce gangrene in.
To destroy the active powers or essential qualities of; to change by chemical action.
q: Quicksilver is mortified with turpentine.
He mortified pearls in vinegar.

senses.d: To deaden by religious or other discipline, as the carnal affections, bodily appetites, or worldly desires; to bring into subjection; to abase; to humble.
q: With fasting mortified, worn out with tears.
Mortify thy learned lust.
Mortify, therefore, your members which are upon the earth.

senses.d: To affect with vexation, chagrin, or humiliation; to humble; to depress.
q: The news of the fatal battle of Worcester, which exceedingly mortified our expectations.
How often is the ambitious man mortified with the very praises he receives, if they do not rise so high as he thinks they ought!

Mortify.etym: [OE. mortifien, F. mortifier, fr. L. mortificare; L. mors, mortis, death + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Mortal, and -fy.]

senses.d: To lose vitality and organic structure, as flesh of a living body; to gangrene.
To practice penance from religious motives; to deaden desires by religious discipline.
q: This makes him . . . give alms of all that he hath, watch, fast, and mortify.

senses.d: To be subdued; to decay, as appetites, desires, etc.
A large flatboat, used in the West Indies for taking freight from shore to ship.
Consisting of the greatest number or quantity; greater in number or quantity than all the rest; nearly all.
q: The cities wherein most of his mighty works were done.

senses.d: Greatest in degree; as, he has the most need of it.
Highest in rank; greatest.
q: A quarter of a year or some months at the most.
A covetous man makes the most of what he has.

Most.etym: [OE. most, mast, mest, AS. mǣst; akin to D. meest, OS. mēst, G. meist, Icel. mestr, Goth. maists; a superl. corresponding to E. more. √103. See More, a.]

senses.d: In the greatest or highest degree.
q: Those nearest to this king, and most his favorites, were courtiers and prelates.
The most unkindest cut of all.
The most straitest sect of our religion.

senses.d: A meeting of persons for discussion; as, a wardmote in the city of London.
A body of persons who meet for discussion, esp. about the management of affairs; as, a folkmote.
A place of meeting for discussion.
The flourish sounded on a horn by a huntsman. See Mot, n., 3, and Mort.
A small particle, as of floating dust; anything proverbially small; a speck.
q: The little motes in the sun do ever stir, though there be no wind.
We are motes in the midst of generations.

senses.d: A mote.
Any nocturnal lepidopterous insect, or any not included among the butterflies; as, the luna moth; Io moth; hawk moth.
Any lepidopterous insect that feeds upon garments, grain, etc.; as, the clothes moth; grain moth; bee moth. See these terms under Clothes, Grain, etc.

Any one of various other insects that destroy woolen and fur goods, etc., esp. the larvæ of several species of beetles of the genera Dermestes and Anthrenus. Carpet moths are often the larvæ of Anthrenus. See Carpet beetle, under Carpet, Dermestes, Anthrenus.
Anything which gradually and silently eats, consumes, or wastes any other thing.

Moth.etym: [OE. mothe, AS. moððe; akin to D. mot, G. motte, Icel. motti, and prob. to E. mad an earthworm. Cf. Mad, n., Mawk.]

senses.d: A female parent; especially, one of the human race; a woman who has borne a child.
That which has produced or nurtured anything; source of birth or origin; generatrix.
q: Alas! poor country! . . . it can not Be called our mother, but our grave.
I behold . . . the solitary majesty of Crete, mother of a religion, it is said, that lived two thousand years.

senses.d: An old woman or matron.
The female superior or head of a religious house, as an abbess, etc.
Hysterical passion; hysteria.

Mother.etym: [OE. moder, AS. mōdor; akin to D. moeder, OS. mōdar, G. mutter, OHG. muotar, Icel. mōðir, Dan. & Sw. moder, OSlav. mati, Russ. mate, Ir. & Gael. mathair, L. mater, Gr. μήτηρ, Skr. mātṛ; cf. Skr. mā to measure. √268. Cf. Material, Matrix, Metropolis, Father.]

senses.d: Received by birth or from ancestors; native, natural; as, mother language; also acting the part, or having the place of a mother; producing others; originating.
q: It is the mother falsehood from which all idolatry is derived.

senses.d: To adopt as a son or daughter; to perform the duties of a mother to.
q: The queen, to have put lady Elizabeth besides the crown, would have mothered another body's child.

senses.d: A film or membrane which is developed on the surface of fermented alcoholic liquids, such as vinegar, wine, etc., and acts as a means of conveying the oxygen of the air to the alcohol and other combustible principles of the liquid, thus leading to their oxidation.

Mother.etym: [Akin to D. modder mud, G. moder mold, mud, Dan. mudder mud, and to E. mud. See Mud.]

senses.d: To become like, or full of, mother, or thick matter, as vinegar.
The act, process, or state of changing place or position; movement; the passing of a body from one place or position to another, whether voluntary or involuntary; — opposed to rest.
q: Speaking or mute, all comeliness and grace attends thee, and each word, each motion, forms.

senses.d: Power of, or capacity for, motion.
q: Devoid of sense and motion.

senses.d: Direction of movement; course; tendency; as, the motion of the planets is from west to east.
q: In our proper motion we ascend.

senses.d: Change in the relative position of the parts of anything; action of a machine with respect to the relative movement of its parts.
q: This is the great wheel to which the clock owes its motion.

senses.d: Movement of the mind, desires, or passions; mental act, or impulse to any action; internal activity.
q: Let a good man obey every good motion rising in his heart, knowing that every such motion proceeds from God.

senses.d: A proposal or suggestion looking to action or progress; esp., a formal proposal made in a deliberative assembly; as, a motion to adjourn.
q: Yes, I agree, and thank you for your motion.

senses.d: An application made to a court or judge orally in open court. Its object is to obtain an order or rule directing some act to be done in favor of the applicant.
Change of pitch in successive sounds, whether in the same part or in groups of parts.
q: The independent motions of different parts sounding together constitute counterpoint.

senses.d: A puppet show or puppet.
q: What motion's this? the model of Nineveh?

Motion.etym: [F., fr. L. motio, fr. movere, motum, to move. See Move.]

senses.d: To make a significant movement or gesture, as with the hand; as, to motion to one to take a seat.
To make proposal; to offer plans.
To direct or invite by a motion, as of the hand or head; as, to motion one to a seat.
To propose; to move.
q: I want friends to motion such a matter.

senses.d: A mass of earth, or earth and rock, rising considerably above the common surface of the surrounding land; a mountain; a high hill; — used always instead of mountain, when put before a proper name; as, Mount Washington; otherwise, chiefly in poetry.
A bulwark for offense or defense; a mound.
q: Hew ye down trees, and cast a mount against Jerusalem.

senses.d: A bank; a fund.

Mount.etym: [OE. munt, mont, mount, AS. munt, fr. L. mons, montis; cf. L. minae protections, E. eminent, menace: cf. F. mont. Cf. Mount, v., Mountain, Mont, Monte, Montem.]

senses.d: To rise on high; to go up; to be upraised or uplifted; to tower aloft; to ascend; — often with up.
q: Though Babylon should mount up to heaven.
The fire of trees and houses mounts on high.

senses.d: To get up on anything, as a platform or scaffold; especially, to seat one's self on a horse for riding.
To attain in value; to amount.
q: Bring then these blessings to a strict account, Make fair deductions, see to what they mount.

Mount.etym: [OE. mounten, monten, F. monter, fr. L. mons, montis, mountain. See Mount, n. (above).]

senses.d: To get upon; to ascend; to climb.
q: Shall we mount again the rural throne?

senses.d: To place one's self on, as a horse or other animal, or anything that one sits upon; to bestride.
To cause to mount; to put on horseback; to furnish with animals for riding; to furnish with horses.

Hence: To put upon anything that sustains and fits for use, as a gun on a carriage, a map or picture on cloth or paper; to prepare for being worn or otherwise used, as a diamond by setting, or a sword blade by adding the hilt, scabbard, etc.
To raise aloft; to lift on high.
q: What power is it which mounts my love so high?

senses.d: That upon which a person or thing is mounted
A horse.
q: She had so good a seat and hand, she might be trusted with any mount.

senses.d: The cardboard or cloth on which a drawing, photograph, or the like is mounted; a mounting.

Any one of seven fleshy prominences in the palm of the hand which are taken as significant of the influence of “planets,” and called the mounts of Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, the Moon, Saturn, the Sun or Apollo, and Venus.
A large mass of earth and rock, rising above the common level of the earth or adjacent land; earth and rock forming an isolated peak or a ridge; an eminence higher than a hill; a mount.
A range, chain, or group of such elevations; as, the White Mountains.
A mountainlike mass; something of great bulk.
q: I should have been a mountain of mummy.

Mountain.etym: [OE. mountaine, montaine, F. montagne, LL. montanea, montania, fr. L. mons, montis, a mountain; cf. montanus belonging to a mountain. See 1st Mount.]

senses.d: Of or pertaining to a mountain or mountains; growing or living on a mountain; found on or peculiar to mountains; among mountains; as, a mountain torrent; mountain pines; mountain goats; mountain air; mountain howitzer.
Like a mountain; mountainous; vast; very great.
q: The high, the mountain majesty of worth.

senses.d: Seated or serving on horseback or similarly; as, mounted police; mounted infantry.
Placed on a suitable support, or fixed in a setting; as, a mounted gun; a mounted map; a mounted gem.
The act of one that mounts.
That by which anything is prepared for use, or set off to advantage; equipment; embellishment; setting; as, the mounting of a sword or diamond.
= Carriage.
To express or to feel grief or sorrow; to grieve; to be sorrowful; to lament; to be in a state of grief or sadness.
q: Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.

senses.d: To wear the customary garb of a mourner.
q: We mourn in black; why mourn we not in blood?
Grieve for an hour, perhaps, then mourn a year.

Mourn.etym: [AS. murnan; akin to OS. mornian, OHG. mornen, Goth. maúrnan.]

senses.d: To grieve for; to lament; to deplore; to bemoan; to bewail.
q: As if he mourned his rival's ill success.
And looking over the hills, I mourn The darling who shall not return.

senses.d: To utter in a mournful manner or voice.
q: The lovelorn nightingale Nightly to thee her sad song mourneth well.

senses.d: The armed or feruled end of a staff; in a sheephook, the end of the staff to which the hook is attached.
One who mourns or is grieved at any misfortune, as the death of a friend.
q: His mourners were two hosts, his friends and foes.
