senses.d: One who attends a funeral as a hired mourner.
q: Mourners were provided to attend the funeral.

senses.d: Full of sorrow; expressing, or intended to express, sorrow; mourning; grieving; sad; also, causing sorrow; saddening; grievous; as, a mournful person; mournful looks, tones, loss.

Mournful.syn: Sorrowful; lugubrious; sad; doleful; heavy; afflictive; grievous; calamitous.

senses.d: The act of sorrowing or expressing grief; lamentation; sorrow.
Garb, drapery, or emblems indicative of grief, esp. clothing or a badge of somber black.
q: The houses to their tops with black were spread, And ev'n the pavements were with mourning hid.

senses.d: Grieving; sorrowing; lamenting.
Employed to express sorrow or grief; worn or used as appropriate to the condition of one bereaved or sorrowing; as, mourning garments; a mourning ring; a mourning pin, and the like.

Any one of numerous species of small rodents belonging to the genus Mus and various related genera of the family Muridæ. The common house mouse (Mus musculus) is found in nearly all countries. The American white-footed, or deer, mouse (Hesperomys leucopus) sometimes lives in houses. See Dormouse, Meadow mouse, under Meadow, and Harvest mouse, under Harvest.
A knob made on a rope with spun yarn or parceling to prevent a running eye from slipping.
A familiar term of endearment.
A dark-colored swelling caused by a blow.
A match used in firing guns or blasting.

Mouse.etym: [OE. mous, mus, AS. mūs, pl. mȳs; akin to D. muis, G. maus, OHG. & Icel. mūs, Dan. muus, Sw. mus, Russ. muishe, L. mus, Gr. μυ̑σ, Skr. mūsh mouse, mush to steal. √277. Cf. Muscle, Musk.]

senses.d: To watch for and catch mice.
To watch for or pursue anything in a sly manner; to pry about, on the lookout for something.
To tear, as a cat devours a mouse.
To furnish with a mouse; to secure by means of a mousing. See Mouse, n., 2.

The opening through which an animal receives food; the aperture between the jaws or between the lips; also, the cavity, containing the tongue and teeth, between the lips and the pharynx; the buccal cavity.
An opening affording entrance or exit; orifice; aperture;
The crosspiece of a bridle bit, which enters the mouth of an animal.
A principal speaker; one who utters the common opinion; a mouthpiece.
q: Every coffeehouse has some particular statesman belonging to it, who is the mouth of the street where he lives.

senses.d: Cry; voice.
Speech; language; testimony.
q: That in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.

senses.d: A wry face; a grimace; a mow.
q: Counterfeit sad looks, Make mouths upon me when I turn my back.
The mouth of them that speak lies shall be stopped.
Whose mouths must be stopped.

Mouth.etym: [OE. mouth, muþ, AS. mūð; akin to D. mond, OS. mūð, G. mund, Icel. muðr, munnr, Sw. mun, Dan. mund, Goth. munþs, and possibly L. mentum chin; or cf. D. muil mouth, muzzle, G. maul, OHG. mūla, Icel. mūli, and Skr. mukha mouth.]

senses.d: To take into the mouth; to seize or grind with the mouth or teeth; to chew; to devour.
To utter with a voice affectedly big or swelling; to speak in a strained or unnaturally sonorous manner.
q: Mouthing out his hollow oes and aes.

senses.d: To form or cleanse with the mouth; to lick, as a bear her cub.
To make mouths at.
To speak with a full, round, or loud, affected voice; to vociferate; to rant.
q: I'll bellow out for Rome, and for my country, And mouth at Cæsar, till I shake the senate.

senses.d: To put mouth to mouth; to kiss.
To make grimaces, esp. in ridicule or contempt.
q: Well I know, when I am gone, How she mouths behind my back.

senses.d: To cause to change place or posture in any manner; to set in motion; to carry, convey, draw, or push from one place to another; to impel; to stir; as, the wind moves a vessel; the horse moves a carriage.
To transfer (a piece or man) from one space or position to another, according to the rules of the game; as, to move a king.
To excite to action by the presentation of motives; to rouse by representation, persuasion, or appeal; to influence.
q: Minds desirous of revenge were not moved with gold.
No female arts his mind could move.

senses.d: To arouse the feelings or passions of; especially, to excite to tenderness or compassion; to touch pathetically; to excite, as an emotion.
q: When he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them.
in orations and poetry is to move pity or terror.

senses.d: To propose; to recommend; specifically, to propose formally for consideration and determination, in a deliberative assembly; to submit, as a resolution to be adopted; as, to move to adjourn.
q: Let me but move one question to your daughter.
They are to be blamed alike who move and who decline war upon particular respects.

senses.d: To apply to, as for aid.

Move.syn: To stir; agitate; trouble; affect; persuade; influence; actuate; impel; rouse; prompt; instigate; incite; induce; incline; propose; offer.
Move.etym: [OE. moven, OF. moveir, F. mouvoir, L. movere; cf. Gr. αμεἴβειν to change, exchange, go in or out, quit, Skr. mīv, p. p. mūta, to move, push. Cf. Emotion, Mew to molt, Mob, Mutable, Mutiny.]

senses.d: To change place or posture; to stir; to go, in any manner, from one place or position to another; as, a ship moves rapidly.
q: The foundations also of the hills moved and were shaken, because he was wroth.
On the green bank I sat and listened long, . . . Nor till her lay was ended could I move.

senses.d: To act; to take action; to stir; to begin to act; as, to move in a matter.
To change residence; to remove, as from one house, town, or state, to another.
To change the place of a piece in accordance with the rules of the game.
The act of moving; a movement.
The act of moving one of the pieces, from one position to another, in the progress of the game.
An act for the attainment of an object; a step in the execution of a plan or purpose.
A person or thing that moves, stirs, or changes place.
A person or thing that imparts motion, or causes change of place; a motor.
One who, or that which, excites, instigates, or causes movement, change, etc.; as, movers of sedition.
q: These most poisonous compounds, Which are the movers of a languishing death.

senses.d: A proposer; one who offers a proposition, or recommends anything for consideration or adoption; as, the mover of a resolution in a legislative body.
Changing place or posture; causing motion or action; as, a moving car, or power.
Exciting movement of the mind; adapted to move the sympathies, passions, or affections; touching; pathetic; as, a moving appeal.
q: I sang an old moving story.

senses.d: The act of changing place or posture; esp., the act of changing one's dwelling place or place of business.
A wry face.

Mow.etym: [F. moue pouting, a wry face; cf. OD. mouwe the protruded lip.]

senses.d: To make mouths.
q: Nodding, becking, and mowing.

senses.d: Same as Mew, a gull.
May; can.
q: Our walles mowe not make hem resistence.

senses.d: To cut down, as grass, with a scythe or machine.
To cut the grass from; as, to mow a meadow.
To cut down; to cause to fall in rows or masses, as in mowing grass; — with down; as, a discharge of grapeshot mows down whole ranks of men.

Mow.etym: [OE. mowen, mawen, AS. māwan; akin to D. maaijen, G. mähen, OHG. mājan, Dan. meie, L. metere to reap, mow, Gr. αμἀ̑ν. Cf. Math, Mead a meadow, Meadow.]

senses.d: To cut grass, etc., with a scythe, or with a machine; to cut grass for hay.
A heap or mass of hay or of sheaves of grain stowed in a barn.
The place in a barn where hay or grain in the sheaf is stowed.
To lay, as hay or sheaves of grain, in a heap or mass in a barn; to pile and stow away.
One who, or that which, mows; a mowing machine; as, a lawn mower.
The act of one who, or the operation of that which, mows.
Land from which grass is cut; meadow land.
Cut down by mowing, as grass; deprived of grass by mowing; as, a mown field.
Great in quantity; long in duration; as, much rain has fallen; much time.
q: Thou shalt carry much seed out into the field, and shalt gather but little in.

senses.d: Many in number.
q: Edom came out against him with much people.

senses.d: High in rank or position.

Much.etym: [OE. moche, muche, miche, prob. the same as mochel, muchel, michel, mikel, fr. AS. micel, mycel; cf. Gr. μέγασ, fem. μεγάλη, great, and Icel. mjök, adv., much. √103. See Mickle.]

senses.d: A great quantity; a great deal; also, an indefinite quantity; as, you have as much as I.
q: He that gathered much had nothing over.

senses.d: A thing uncommon, wonderful, or noticeable; something considerable.
q: And thought not much to clothe his enemies.

senses.d: To a great degree or extent; greatly; abundantly; far; nearly.
q: Thou art much mightier than we.
Excellent speech becometh not a fool, much less do lying lips a prince.
Henceforth I fly not death, nor would prolong Life much.
All left the world much as they found it.

senses.d: Anything used in muffling; esp., a scarf for protecting the head and neck in cold weather; a tippet.
q: Fortune is painted blind, with a muffler above her eyes.

senses.d: A cushion for terminating or softening a note made by a stringed instrument with a keyboard.
A kind of mitten or boxing glove, esp. when stuffed.
One who muffles.

Any of various devices to deaden the noise of escaping gases or vapors, as a tube filled with obstructions, through which the exhaust gases of an internal-combustion engine, as on an automobile, are passed (called also silencer).
The berry or fruit of any tree of the genus Morus; also, the tree itself. See Morus.
A dark pure color, like the hue of a black mulberry.

Mulberry.etym: [OE. moolbery, murberie, AS. murberie, where the first part is fr. L. morum mulberry; cf. Gr. �, �. Cf. Murrey, Sycamore.]

senses.d: A hybrid animal; specifically, one generated between an ass and a mare, sometimes a horse and a she-ass. See Hinny.
A plant or vegetable produced by impregnating the pistil of one species with the pollen or fecundating dust of another; — called also hybrid.
A very stubborn person.
A machine, used in factories, for spinning cotton, wool, etc., into yarn or thread and winding it into cops; — called also jenny and mule-jenny.

Mule.etym: [F., a she-mule, L. mula, fem. of mulus; cf. Gr. μύκλοσ, μυχλόσ. Cf. AS. mūl, fr. L. mulus. Cf. Mulatto.]

senses.d: To increase in number; to make more numerous; to add quantity to.
q: Impunity will multiply motives to disobedience.

senses.d: To add (any given number or quantity) to itself a certain number of times; to find the product of by multiplication; thus 7 multiplied by 8 produces the number 56; to multiply two numbers. See the Note under Multiplication.
To increase (the amount of gold or silver) by the arts of alchemy.

Multiply.etym: [F. multiplier, L. multiplicare, fr. multiplex manifold. See Multitude, Complex.]

senses.d: To become greater in number; to become numerous.
q: When men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them.

senses.d: To increase in extent and influence; to spread.
q: The word of God grew and multiplied.

senses.d: To increase amount of gold or silver by the arts of alchemy.
A great number of persons collected together; a numerous collection of persons; a crowd; an assembly.
q: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them.

senses.d: A great number of persons or things, regarded collectively; as, the book will be read by a multitude of people; the multitude of stars; a multitude of cares.
q: It is a fault in a multitude of preachers, that they utterly neglect method in their harangues.
A multitude of flowers As countless as the stars on high.

senses.d: The state of being many; numerousness.
q: They came as grasshoppers for multitude.

Multitude.syn: Throng; crowd; assembly; assemblage; commonalty; swarm; populace; vulgar. See Throng.
Multitude.etym: [F. multitude, L. multitudo, multitudinis, fr. multus much, many; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: Fortification; stronghold.
q: His place of defense shall be the munitions of rocks.

senses.d: Whatever materials are used in war for defense or for annoying an enemy; ammunition; also, stores and provisions; military stores of all kinds.
q: The bodies of men, munition, and money, may justly be called the sinews of war.

Munition.etym: [F., munition of war, L. munitio a fortifying, fortification, fr. munire to fortify, defend with a wall; cf. moenia walls, murus (for moirus) a wall, and Skr. mi to fix, make firm. Cf. Ammunition.]

senses.d: The offense of killing a human being with malice prepense or aforethought, express or implied; intentional and unlawful homicide.
q: The killing of their children had, in the account of God, the guilt of murder, as the offering them to idols had the guilt of idolatry.
Slaughter grows murder when it goes too far.

Murder.etym: [OE. morder, morther, AS. morðor, fr. morð murder; akin to D. moord, OS. morð, G., Dan., & Sw. mord, Icel. morð, Goth. maúrþr, OSlav. mrēti to die, Lith. mirti, W. marw dead, L. mors, mortis, death, mori, moriri, to die, Gr. βροτόσ (for μροτόσ) mortal, ἄμβροτοσ immortal, Skr. mṛ to die, mṛta death.

senses.d: To kill with premediated malice; to kill (a human being) willfully, deliberately, and unlawfully. See Murder, n.
To destroy; to put an end to.
q: murder thy breath in middle of a word?

senses.d: To mutilate, spoil, or deform, as if with malice or cruelty; to mangle; as, to murder the king's English.

Murder.syn: To kill; assassinate; slay. See Kill.
Murder.etym: [OE. mortheren, murtheren, AS. myrðrian; akin to OHG. murdiren, Goth. maúrþrjan. See Murder, n.]

senses.d: One guilty of murder; a person who, in possession of his reason, unlawfully kills a human being with premeditated malice.
A small cannon, formerly used for clearing a ship's decks of boarders; — called also murdering piece.
A low, confused, and indistinct sound, like that of running water.
A complaint half suppressed, or uttered in a low, muttering voice.
q: Some discontents there are, some idle murmurs.

Murmur.etym: [F. murmure: cf. L. murmur. CF. Murmur, v. i.]

senses.d: To make a low continued noise, like the hum of bees, a stream of water, distant waves, or the wind in a forest.
q: They murmured as doth a swarm of bees.

senses.d: To utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice; to feel or express dissatisfaction or discontent; to grumble; — often with at or against.
q: And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron.
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured.

Murmur.etym: [F. murmurer, L. murmurare, murmurari, fr. murmur murmur; cf. Gr.� to roar and boil, said of water, Skr. marmara a rustling sound; prob. of imitative origin.]

senses.d: To utter or give forth in low or indistinct words or sounds; as, to murmur tales.
q: The people murmured such things concerning him.

senses.d: One who murmurs.
Uttering murmurs; making low sounds; complaining.
An infectious and fatal disease among cattle.

Murrain.etym: [OE. moreine, OF. morine, fr. OF. morir, murir, 8die, L. mori, moriri.]

senses.d: Having, or afflicted with, murrain.
A genus of small rodents, including the common mouse and rat.
A gap or hole in a hedge, hence, wall, or the like, through which a wild animal is accustomed to pass; a muset.
q: Find a hare without a muse.

senses.d: One of the nine goddesses who presided over song and the different kinds of poetry, and also the arts and sciences; — often used in the plural.
q: Granville commands; your aid, O Muses, bring: What Muse for Granville can refuse to sing?

senses.d: A particular power and practice of poetry.
A poet; a bard.

Muse.etym: [F. Muse, L. Musa, Gr. �. Cf. Mosaic, n., Music.]

senses.d: To think closely; to study in silence; to meditate.
q: He mused upon some dangerous plot.

senses.d: To be absent in mind; to be so occupied in study or contemplation as not to observe passing scenes or things present; to be in a brown study.
To wonder.

Muse.syn: To consider; meditate; ruminate. See Ponder.
Muse.etym: [F. muser to loiter or trifle, orig., to stand with open mouth, fr. LL. musus, morsus, muzzle, snout, fr. L. morsus a biting, bite, fr. mordere to bite. See Morsel, and cf. Amuse, Muzzle, n.]

senses.d: To think on; to meditate on.
q: Come, then, expressive Silence, muse his praise.

senses.d: To wonder at.
Contemplation which abstracts the mind from passing scenes; absorbing thought; hence, absence of mind; a brown study.
Wonder, or admiration.

Of or pertaining to music; having the qualities of music; or the power of producing music; devoted to music; melodious; harmonious; as, musical proportion; a musical voice; musical instruments; a musical sentence; musical persons.
Music.
q: To fetch home May with their musical.

senses.d: A social entertainment of which music is the leading feature; a musical party.
One skilled in the art or science of music; esp., a skilled singer, or performer on a musical instrument.
To be obliged; to be necessitated; — expressing either physical or moral necessity; as, a man must eat for nourishment; we must submit to the laws.
To be morally required; to be necessary or essential to a certain quality, character, end, or result; as, he must reconsider the matter; he must have been insane.
q: Likewise must the deacons be grave.
Morover, he must have a good report of them which are without.

Must.etym: [OE. moste, a pret. generally meaning, could, was free to, pres. mot, moot, AS. mōste, pret. mōt, pres.; akin to D. moetan to be obliged, OS. mōtan to be free, to be obliged, OHG. muozan, G. müssen to be obliged, Sw. måste must, Goth. gamōtan to have place, have room, to able; of unknown origin.]

senses.d: The expressed juice of the grape, or other fruit, before fermentation.
q: No fermenting must fills . . . the deep vats.

senses.d: Mustiness.

Must.etym: [AS. must, fr. L. mustum (sc. vinum), from mustus young, new, fresh. Cf. Mustard.]

senses.d: To make musty; to become musty.
Being in a condition of dangerous frenzy, usually connected with sexual excitement; — said of adult male elephants which become so at irregular intervals.
The condition of frenzy.

Must.etym: [Hind. mast intoxicated, ruttish, fr. Skr. matta, p.p. of mad to rejoice, intoxicate.]

senses.d: The name of several cruciferous plants of the genus Brassica (formerly Sinapis), as white mustard (B. alba), black mustard (B. Nigra), wild mustard or charlock (B. Sinapistrum).
A powder or a paste made from the seeds of black or white mustard, used as a condiment and a rubefacient. Taken internally it is stimulant and diuretic, and in large doses is emetic.

Mustard.etym: [OF. moustarde, F. moutarde, fr. L. mustum must, — mustard was prepared for use by being mixed with must. See Must, n.]

senses.d: Something shown for imitation; a pattern.
A show; a display.
An assembling or review of troops, as for parade, verification of numbers, inspection, exercise, or introduction into service.
q: The hurried muster of the soldiers of liberty.
See how in warlike muster they appear, In rhombs, and wedges, and half-moons, and wings.

senses.d: The sum total of an army when assembled for review and inspection; the whole number of effective men in an army.
q: And the muster was thirty thousands of men.
Ye publish the musters of your own bands, and proclaim them to amount of thousands.

senses.d: Any assemblage or display; a gathering.
q: Of the temporal grandees of the realm, mentof their wives and daughters, the muster was great and splendid.
Such excuses will not pass muster with God.

Muster.etym: [OE. moustre, OF. mostre, moustre, F. montre, LL. monstra. See Muster, v. t.]

senses.d: To collect and display; to assemble, as troops for parade, inspection, exercise, or the like.
Hence: To summon together; to enroll in service; to get together.
q: All the gay feathers he could muster.
One of those who can muster up sufficient sprightliness to engage in a game of forfeits.

Muster.etym: [OE. mustren, prop., to show, OF. mostrer, mustrer, moustrer, monstrer, F. montrer, fr. L. monstrare to show. See Monster.]

senses.d: To be gathered together for parade, inspection, exercise, or the like; to come together as parts of a force or body; as, his supporters mustered in force.
To utter words indistinctly or with a low voice and lips partly closed; esp., to utter indistinct complaints or angry expressions; to grumble; to growl.
q: Wizards that peep, and that mutter.
Meantime your filthy foreigner will stare, And mutter to himself.

senses.d: To sound with a low, rumbling noise.
q: Thick lightnings flash, the muttering thunder rolls.

Mutter.etym: [Prob. of imitative origin; cf. L. muttire, mutire.]

senses.d: To utter with imperfect articulations, or with a low voice; as, to mutter threats.
Repressed or obscure utterance.
Reciprocally acting or related; reciprocally receiving and giving; reciprocally given and received; reciprocal; interchanged; as, a mutual love, advantage, assistance, aversion, etc.
q: Conspiracy and mutual promise.
Happy in our mutual help, And mutual love.
A certain shyness on such subjects, which was mutual between the sisters.

senses.d: Possessed, experienced, or done by two or more persons or things at the same time; common; joint; as, mutual happiness; a mutual effort.
q: A vast accession of misery and woe from the mutual weeping, and wailing, and gnashing of teeth.

Mutual.etym: [F. mutuel, L. mutuus, orig., exchanged, borrowed, lent; akin to mutare to change. See Mutable.]

senses.d: The projecting mouth and nose of a quadruped, as of a horse; a snout.
The mouth of a thing; the end for entrance or discharge; as, the muzzle of a gun.
A fastening or covering (as a band or cage) for the mouth of an animal, to prevent eating or vicious biting.
q: With golden muzzles all their mouths were bound

Muzzle.etym: [OE. mosel, OF. musel, F. museau muzzle or snout, LL. musellus, fr. musus, morsus. See Muse, v. i., and cf. Morsel.]

senses.d: To bind the mouth of; to fasten the mouth of, so as to prevent biting or eating; hence, figuratively, to bind; to sheathe; to restrain from speech or action.
q: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.

senses.d: To fondle with the closed mouth.
To bring the mouth or muzzle near.
q: The bear muzzles and smells to him.

senses.d: Of or belonging to me; — used always attributively; as, my body; my book; — mine is used in the predicate; as, the book is mine. See Mine.

My.etym: [OE. mi, fr. min. See Mine, and cf., for loss of n, A, a., An, a.]

senses.d: A gum resin, usually of a yellowish brown or amber color, of an aromatic odor, and a bitter, slightly pungent taste. It is valued for its odor and for its medicinal properties. It exudes from the bark of a shrub of Abyssinia and Arabia, the Balsamodendron Myrrha. The myrrh of the Bible is supposed to have been partly the gum above named, and partly the exudation of species of Cistus, or rockrose.

Myrrh.etym: [OE. mirre, OF. mirre, F. myrrhe, L. myrrha, murra, Gr. �; cf. Ar. murr bitter, also myrrh, Heb. mar bitter.]

senses.d: A species of the genus Myrtus, especially Myrtus communis. The common myrtle has a shrubby, upright stem, eight or ten feet high. Its branches form a close, full head, thickly covered with ovate or lanceolate evergreen leaves. It has solitary axillary white or rosy flowers, followed by black several-seeded berries. The ancients considered it sacred to Venus. The flowers, leaves, and berries are used variously in perfumery and as a condiment, and the beautifully mottled wood is used in turning.

Myrtle.etym: [F. myrtil bilberry, prop., a little myrtle, from myrte myrtle, L. myrtus, murtus, Gr. μύρτοσ; cf. Per. mūrd.]

senses.d: I or me in person; — used for emphasis, my own self or person; as I myself will do it; I have done it myself; — used also instead of me, as the object of the first person of a reflexive verb, without emphasis; as, I will defend myself.

A profound secret; something wholly unknown, or something kept cautiously concealed, and therefore exciting curiosity or wonder; something which has not been or can not be explained; hence, specifically, that which is beyond human comprehension.
q: We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery.

If God should please to reveal unto us this great mystery of the Trinity, or some other mysteries in our holy religion, we should not be able to understand them, unless he would bestow on us some new faculties of the mind.

senses.d: A kind of secret religious celebration, to which none were admitted except those who had been initiated by certain preparatory ceremonies; — usually plural; as, the Eleusinian mysteries.
The consecrated elements in the eucharist.
Anything artfully made difficult; an enigma.

Mystery.etym: [L. mysterium, Gr. μυστήριον, fr. μύστησ one initiated in mysteries; cf. μυει̑ν to initiate into the mysteries, fr. μύειν to shut the eyes. Cf. Mute, a.]

senses.d: A trade; a handicraft; hence, any business with which one is usually occupied.
q: Fie upon him, he will discredit our mystery.
And that which is the noblest mystery Brings to reproach and common infamy.

senses.d: A dramatic representation of a Scriptural subject, often some event in the life of Christ; a dramatic composition of this character; as, the Chester Mysteries, consisting of dramas acted by various craft associations in that city in the early part of the 14th century.
q: “Mystery plays,” so called because acted by craftsmen.

Mystery.etym: [OE. mistere, OF. mestier, F. métier, L. ministerium. See Ministry.]

senses.d: The badge of a family, esp. of a family of the ancient feudal nobility. The most frequent form of the mon is circular, and it commonly consists of conventionalized forms from nature, flowers, birds, insects, the lightnings, the waves of the sea, or of geometrical symbolic figures; color is only a secondary character. It appears on lacquer and pottery, and embroidered on, or woven in, fabrics. The imperial chrysanthemum, the mon of the reigning family, is used as a national emblem. Formerly the mon of the shoguns of the Tokugawa family was so used.
